World.title: Alleged operator of major darknet drugs platform charged in Germany
World.content:
More than a year after authorities took down the darknet marketplace “Archetyp Market,” German prosecutors have charged the alleged operator of the platform, which was reportedly used for the large-scale trading of illegal substances.

 

The 31-year-old suspect is accused of having run the platform since July 2020, facilitating the sale of narcotics and other illegal substances.

Prosecutors allege that, from June 2022 onward, he operated the marketplace as part of an organized criminal group involving at least two other people, generating around €20 million in revenue.

At the time it was shut down in June 2025, Archetyp was the world's largest darknet marketplace for illegal drugs.

The platform offered a wide range of substances, including cocaine, heroin, crystal meth, fentanyl, and crack cocaine. It also hosted listings for cannabis products, prescription drugs, performance-enhancing substances, and new psychoactive drugs.

Between November 2022 and June 2025 alone, around 2.3 million orders were processed on the platform, with an estimated turnover of about €330 million.

According to the indictment, the man set up and operated the platform's technical infrastructure. He is also alleged to have determined the marketplace's strategic direction and enabled vendors to trade in illegal goods.

More than 600,000 customer accounts were registered on the platform. The cryptocurrency Monero is said to have been used as a payment method, with the operator allegedly receiving a 5% commission on each sale.

The investigation took place as part of the international operation "Deep Sentinel", which was coordinated by the Central Office for Combating Cybercrime and the Federal Criminal Police Office. German authorities were supported by Europol and Eurojust.

As part of the investigation, authorities seized suspected criminal proceeds, including cryptocurrency, cash, and luxury vehicles, with a combined value of nearly €10 million.

If convicted, the suspect faces up to 15 years in prison, in addition to the confiscation of the seized assets. He was arrested at his home in Barcelona in June 2025 by a special unit of the Spanish National Police and was later extradited to Germany.

World.title: Thousands of migrants, including more than 860 minors, remain in Ceuta
World.content:
Authorities in Ceuta are struggling to cope with thousands of people that remain in the autonomous city following the mass arrival of migrants last week.

 

Security forces estimate that around 73,500 people have already left the North African exclave and returned to Morocco, while local authorities say up to 5,000 remain in the Spanish territory, including 862 minors.

The crisis has so far resulted in at least 88 confirmed deaths, according to Ceuta’s authorities, in addition to bodies recovered by Moroccan authorities in Moroccan waters.

Juan Vivas, the president of Ceuta, estimates that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the city four days after the mass influx from Morocco. He said the situation has not yet returned to normal and that Ceuta is still dealing with the aftermath of the incident.

Vivas added that between 1,800 and 2,000 people had already entered the city by swimming in the days before the mass crossing, a warning sign that he said showed the need for stronger border monitoring and better coordination to prevent another such crisis.

The Ceuta leader also highlighted the emotional toll of the crisis on residents, describing the fear, uncertainty, and sense of helplessness some had experienced. In an interview with Spanish newspaper El País, Vivas said: “Morocco has shown that it cannot be trusted; we must demand respect from it.”

More than 860 minors remain

Ceuta is seeking to expand its reception capacity to care for the 862 minors currently left under the city's watch.

Authorities say the figure could approach one thousand and admit that some may still be on the streets and unaccounted for.

While new facilities are being prepared, existing shelters are operating beyond their capacity. The Spanish territory is continuing to offer support for the minors and is preparing new reception measures while it processes possible transfers to mainland Spain.

City services have increased support, providing accommodation, food and clothing. Younger children have been placed in more suitable facilities, while older teenagers are being housed in temporary spaces until more resources become available.

Caring for minors has become one of the city's main priorities, with around 250 workers assigned to the task. Officials do not rule out further increases in the number of children under the city’s care. Drawing on the experience of the 2021 migration crisis, the Ceuta government estimates the figure could eventually reach between 1,000 and 1,100 minors.

The city’s reception system is completely overwhelmed. Its 29 standard places for minors are currently operating at almost 3,000% of their capacity. The local government is calling on the Spanish state to provide urgent assistance and additional funding, while preparing new facilities, including an industrial warehouse in El Tarajal, to cope with the arrivals.

Ceuta residents take action amid growing uncertainty

Fears of further incidents following the mass arrivals have prompted some residents of Ceuta to set up barriers in the territory, installing makeshift fences to restrict access to certain streets.

Tensions have risen in several parts of the city in recent days, with residents reporting isolated incidents and confrontations, according to El Faro de Ceuta. In one neighborhood, a resident claimed he was assaulted after refusing to give a cigarette, while some young migrants said they regretted that the actions of a small number of individuals were affecting the image of the wider group.

World.title: Ceuta migration crisis sparks protests as Spanish government faces criticism
World.content:
The Ceuta migrant crisis spilled over this weekend into a mass protest in the exclave's Plaza de los Reyes, with hundreds of residents gathering to demand tighter border controls following the arrival of tens of thousands of migrants from Morocco last week.

 

The protest, which was organised on social media, featured chants defending the autonomous city and criticism of the Spanish government's handling of the crisis.

Tensions rose at the event with the arrival of far-right activist Vito Quiles, Se Acabó La Fiesta leader Alvise Pérez, and members of far-right groups such as Núcleo Nacional.

Their presence was met with backlash from some attendees and from some taking part in a parallel counterdemonstration, who accused them of trying to capitalise on the crisis for political gain and of fuelling confrontation.

Some citizens of Ceuta, including many residents of Moroccan origin, held a counterprotest in the same square to defend coexistence in the city and to reject xenophobic rhetoric. For several minutes, both groups exchanged chants and accusations, although no serious incidents were reported.

Rising tensions and heavy police presence

In response, the National Police deployed a large security operation.

Pérez and several members of Núcleo Nacional were escorted to the port, while Quiles left the protest to boos from some of the crowd.

The square remained cordoned off as officers kept the two groups of demonstrators apart.

Despite the tense atmosphere, both the protest and the counterprotest gradually dispersed without the need for a larger police intervention.

World.title: Ceuta explained: How Spain's biggest migration crisis unfolded
World.content:
An unprecedented migration crisis unfolded in Ceuta last Wednesday and escalated dramatically on Thursday, when tens of thousands of people entered the Spanish enclave illegally.

 

In the end, between 60,000 to more than 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Cueta, marking the territory's largest migration crisis. Footage showed thousands of people swimming, navigating around breakwaters or climbing down steep areas in the autonomous city.

The influx prompted Spain to deploy its military and police to contain the situation. Most of those who had entered the North African enclave returned to Morocco within hours, largely due to a lack of accommodation and basic supplies.

Most of the new arrivals were young men, but the footage also showed women with children and entire families, on a journey fraught with the risk of drowning and exhaustion.

At least 88 people died, Spanish officials said on Monday, though Moroccan officials later presented a lower estimate.

Amid criticism from Ceuta's president, Juan Jesús Vivas, as well as growing calls to amend immigration laws to allow for immediate push backs of those who crossed by swimming, Spain and Morocco reached an agreement to speed up the repatriation of migrants.

Spanish army soldiers alongside migrants who swam from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday 1 August 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

The Spanish government and Moroccan authorities have attributed the surge to rumours circulating on social media that falsely claimed a recent Supreme Court ruling prevented the immediate return of migrants, as well as to the activities of people-smuggling networks.

What neither side has adequately explained is why, according to reports from the area, Moroccan security forces initially allowed large crowds to advance towards the border unhindered, or how thousands of people from Casablanca, Rabat, Tangier and Marrakech were able to travel north without the closure of access routes.

The delayed intervention of Moroccan authorities only fuelled suspicions that the surge was coordinated from within.

Migrants who crossed into Spain are escorted by Spanish soldiers towards the Spanish-Moroccan border for their return to Morocco on 2 August 2026. AP PhotoFoto AP/Bernat Armangue

The New York Times reported accounts from several young men explaining how the country's authorities encouraged them to cross into the Spanish city.

Alaoui, 26, said that when his group approached the border on Thursday, several Moroccan police officers pointed them in the right direction, telling them to "go that way, go that way," the US outlet reported.

Spain's Civil Guard reportedly spotted Moroccan intelligence agents among the group of migrants

Sources within Spain's Civil Guard also claimed that officials from Morocco's intelligence service had infiltrated the crowds entering Ceuta.

According to 'El Español' (source in Spanish), they were able to detect so through a camera surveillance system installed at the Ceuta border. Civil Guard analysts identified several individuals operating on the ground, dressed in civilian clothes and mingling with groups of migrants, acting as guides, gathering information and coordinating the crossings.

A migrant who has crossed from Morocco into Spain drinks water distributed by Spanish soldiers in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Sunday 2 August 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

If accurate, these findings challenge the theory that the surge was a spontaneous phenomenon driven largely by social-media rumours and instead suggests a degree of cooperation involving state intelligence actors.

Who was pulling the strings inside Morocco?

According to Spanish newspaper 'The Objective' (source in Spanish), which cited Moroccan sources familiar with the kingdom's power structures, the man identified as the possible mastermind of the operation is Fouad Ali El Himma, a close friend and advisor to King Mohammed VI who is described in some circles as Morocco's 'viceroy'.

A former senior Interior Ministry official and founder of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) in 2008, El Himma is said to have sought to exploit the migration chaos for a dual purpose: to weaken the government of Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch and to strengthen PAM's position ahead of Morocco's general elections.

This timing would not be accidental. On Wednesday, Mohammed VI delivered a speech marking the 27th anniversary of his accession to the throne, projecting an image of stability and progress.

Hours later, thousands of Moroccans were attempting to reach Ceuta, highlighting the stark contrast between the speech and the scenes at the borders.

Supporters of this theory point to events of 2021, when about 10,000 people entered Ceuta after Moroccan forces relaxed border surveillance during the diplomatic crisis sparked by Spain's decision to admit Polisario Front leader Brahim Ghali for hospital treatment.

This instance demonstrated Rabat's ability to control migration flows in ways that can exert political pressure on Spain.

Soldiers from the Spanish army travel in military vehicles after being deployed in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Thursday 30 July 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

Migration as a bargaining chip and Pedro Sánchez's role in Spain's relations with Morocco

Spain has a long history of migration tensions along its southern border, but the Ceuta crisis cannot be understood without consiering the complex relationship between Madrid and Rabat, nor without the disagreements between Pedro Sánchez's government and several of its European partners over migration policy.

In 2022, Sánchez endorsed Morocco's autonomy plan for Western Sahara, backed by the United States. The move—which marked a historic shift from Spain's traditional position of neutrality—was welcomed in Rabat and widely criticised in Spain, including by the Polisario Front and by some parties within the coalition government.

The mass regularisation of migrants driven by the Spanish government has also triggered an open conflict with leaders from 22 European Union countries, who signed a letter explicitly linking that policy to the so-called pull factor and to the Ceuta crisis.

From Italy, Meloni justified the joint letter by saying that "defending borders is a shared responsibility". Italy itself last week introduced stricter temporary Schengen controls for non-EU citizens travelling from Spain.

It is worth noting that the European Union offered to deploy the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in Ceuta, given the gravity of the situation, but the Spanish government rejected the offer.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the return to Morocco of most of those who crossed into Ceuta. However, tensions between Madrid and Brussels remain high.

Pedro Sánchez sent a letter to Brussels criticising the "lack of solidarity" of some EU partners. The letter contained no mention of Morocco's responsibility for the crisis. The Socialist leader also requested an emergency videoconference of EU interior ministers.

The Trump factor: facts and context behind Washington's role

Days before the Ceuta crisis, US President Donald Trump sent a message to Mohammed VI for the occasion of Throne Day, reaffirming Washington's recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and calling Morocco's autonomy proposal "the only basis for reaching a fair and lasting solution".

The message came just days after Morocco named one of its main motorways after the US president.

In April 2026, a Capitol committee approved a budget proposal that included a non-binding recommendation calling on the US diplomatic service to open discussions on Ceuta and Melilla, arguing that the two lie in "Moroccan territory". The proposal received 35 votes in favour, all from Republican members, and 27 against.

During the crisis in Ceuta, the Trump administration has used its platform to warn for the risks of illegal immigration and of laws that fail to curb migrant flows, blaming the "far left" for the situation. One of the few voices to focus on Morocco's responsibility was Anna Paulina Luna, a member of the House of Representatives for the Republican Party.

According to correspondent David Alandete (source in Spanish), the Republican Party's closer ties with Morocco responds to a clear strategic logic: Rabat has demonstrated its willingness to take significant steps to strengthen its relationship with Washington, from recognising Israel to allowing the port of Tangier to be used by arms-carrying ships, naming a road in Western Sahara after Trump and cooperating militarily when requested.

Meanwhile, Pedro Sánchez's government has increasingly become a more difficult partner for Washington, amid repeated disagreements over the war in Gaza, NATO defence spending and the recognition of Palestine.

According to Alandete, US officials don't doubt that Morocco has at times used irregular migration as a means of applying pressure, but there is little political appetite in Washington to back Sánchez against Rabat.

A historical footnote provides further context: in 1967, dictator Francisco Franco warned US President Lyndon B. Johnson in a letter about the risks of rearming Morocco, describing it as an "aggressive and destabilising" nation.

Decades later, former Prime Minister Adolfo Suárez responded to Moroccan threats to annex Ceuta and Melilla with a direct warning: "You know we can bomb Rabat within 48 hours". This approach to managing pressure from Spain's southern neighbour stands in stark contrast to the current government's stance.

The strategic position of Gibraltar: is the control of the Strait of Hormuz what is really at stake?

Several European geopolitical analysts, including French commentator Laurent Ozon (source in Spanish) and historian Édouard Husson, have recently argued that the Ceuta crisis goes beyond the question of migration or internal power struggles in Morocco.

Their main argument is that, with the Strait of Hormuz under growing strain following the joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, as well as pressures on the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, the Strait of Gibraltar—whose territorial waters are under Spanish sovereignty—is gaining exceptional strategic value as the only secure access route to the Mediterranean for international shipping.

According to this interpretation, the United States and Israel would be seeking to establish an alternative corridor through Morocco that would not rely on Spain or, by extension, on the wider European alliance. Under this scenario, Ceuta would be a key asset: control over the city would enable Rabat, acting as a proxy power for the Washington-Tel Aviv axis, to challenge Spain's control of the gateway to the Mediterranean.

Spanish police officers intervene as migrants cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Thursday 30 July 2026. Foto AP/Antonio Sempere

Ozon also argues that European anti-immigration right-wing parties and certain media outlets are, consciously or not, helping to isolate Spain by framing the issue solely around migration policy while overlooking the wider European interest in preserving Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta.

However, this hypothesis, which is gaining traction in certain European geopolitical circles, is not currently backed by any official documentation. It should be read as an interpretative framework proposed by analysts.

A crisis contained but far from over

The Ceuta crisis cannot be viewed as an isolated event. It is the latest development in a broader sequence of events, which includes the 2021 migration incident, Spain's shift in position on Western Sahara, allegations that Pegasus spyware was used against Spanish government officials from Morocco, ignored warnings from the CNI intelligence service, mass migrant regularisation and the gradual deterioration of Spain's standing in its relations with Washington and Brussels.

But beyond the competing theories, several points remain clear: Morocco has once again demonstrated its ability to influence migration flows; that, according to police intelligence sources, Spanish authorities were warned and did not act; that at least 88 people have lost their lives attempting the crossing and that hundreds remain in Ceuta with no short-term solution in sight.

Many local residents have voiced their frustration over the government's response to a situation that is not new, and which they say makes them feel unsafe and unprotected.

Residents of Ceuta protest against the arrival of Spanish far-right politician Alvise Pérez in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Saturday 1 August 2026. Foto AP/Bernat Armangue

Spain's King Felipe VI also sought to send a message of suppor to the people of Ceuta, expressing his "indignation" and recalling that "the state must safeguard the security of Ceuta and Melilla".

The question now facing Spain, is whether the country still has the capacity and political will to manage its southern border with relying on Morocco's cooperation, and whether the European bloc can maintain a united response when crises like last week's in Ceuta emerge again.

World.title: England and Wales record driest July on record, Met Office says
World.content:
England and Wales recorded their driest July on record this year, the UK's national weather agency has announced, citing provisional figures.

 

The Met Office described July as an "exceptional month" for the UK's weather books, with provisional statistics showing records were challenged or broken for temperature, sunshine, and rainfall.

According to the agency, England saw 6.5mm of rainfall over the month of July, 10% of its usual average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm, which was set in 1911.

Southern England also experienced its "driest month ever recorded" in July, the Met Office added, noting that records dated back to 1836.

In Wales, 9.3mm of rainfall was recorded in July, around 9% of the normal average and again less than half of the previous record of 22.6mm - also set in 1911.

Dr. Amy Doherty, a science manager at the Met Office, called July a "truly remarkable month in the UK's climate record."

“The combination of record-breaking dryness, exceptional warmth and unprecedented sunshine has delivered one of the most notable summer months in our historical records," she said.

Europe's scorching summer

Much of Europe has sweltered under high temperatures this summer, with brutal heatwaves wreaking havoc across the continent - which has been battling devastating wildfires and severe droughts.

A pharmacy display shows a temperature of 43 degrees Celsius in Paris during a heat wave, Wednesday, July 29, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Emergency services and hospitals have been pushed to their limits amid repeated surges in callouts linked to the hot weather, and many countries have reported increases in heat-related deaths. In July, the UK Health Security Agency said there were estimated to have been around 2,877 heat-associated deaths in England during two hot spells in May and June.

Soaring temperatures are now also adding to concerns of an energy crisis in central Europe, where the Danube River has dropped to record-low levels.

In Hungary, a fresh heatwave almost forced the shutdown of the nation's only nuclear power plant for the first time in 44 years, although Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Monday that it was still in operation for the time being.

World.title: Study shows why younger generations may be more cancer-prone
World.content:
Researchers are observing certain age-related types of cancer more frequently in younger people. A new study suggests this could be because younger generations are aging faster than their parents or grandparents.

Susanna was just 28 years old when she was diagnosed with bowel cancer. Andre developed lung cancer when he was only 34. Both of them have turned to social media to talk about their fight against the disease. Neither of them are medical outliers — not anymore.

The German Cancer Research Center (DKFZ) has reported a sharp increase in gastrointestinal cancer cases for patients between the ages of 20 and 39. In the US, researchers have observed a similar development, with an even higher disease ratio than in Germany. Younger people are also increasingly being diagnosed with other types of cancers, including those that affect patients' bone marrow or uterus.

Cancer is usually regarded as an age-related disease. According to the German Cancer Aid non-profit, the average age for men and women with cancer is around 69. Cancer cells form when certain sections of the genetic sequence mutate and can no longer be repaired. The older we get, the less reliable our repair system becomes.

Making cancer cell therapy affordable To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Gap between chronologal and biological gap increasing

A study by researchers at Washington University School of Medicine, US, has now found a link that could help explain why an increasing number of people under 50 are developing early-onset cancer. The reason, they suggest, is that younger generations are displaying a wider gap between their biological and their chronological ages. In short, they are aging faster.

While the chronological age counts how many years have passed since a person's birth, their biological age describes how much their body has aged, based on the cellular damage accumulated. Individual organs and tissues can age at varying speeds.

In other words, the same person's liver, heart and brain could each have different biological ages, all of which could differ still from the person's actual age.

The recent study has now for the first time established a link between the increasing gap between biological and chronological ages in younger generations on the one hand, and the risk of early-onset cancer on the other, Ron Jachimowicz explains. He's an attending physician and hematologist at the University Hospital Cologne, as well as head of the Max Planck Research Group for Biology of Aging.

"Don't forget, this is a correlative study," Jachomowicz cautions.

Correlation refers to two things appearing in concert, so it looks like they are related. It does not prove causation, which we speak of when one factor causes another.

While results can provide certain indications that seem quite plausible, researchers were already well aware of the fact "that there is an association between biological age and the risk of developing cancer," Jachomowicz says.

Here's what you need to know about breast cancer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DNA, bloodmarkers and telomeres: How to determine one's biological age

It's not easy to determine a person's biological age. Calculating it requires a number of parameters — there is no single, precise test. Instead, epigenetic tests are used to determine chemical alterations of DNA sequences, evaluating certain blood values and measuring the length of so-called telomeres — that is, the repetitive DNA sequence located at the end of chromosomes that function as protective caps.

There are also physiological tests, to monitor various body and organ functions, as well as cognitive evaluations.

Researchers in the study at hand applied a combination of these various measurement techniques to analyze the data of more than 150,000 individuals drawn from the UK Biobank, a British biometric dataset.

They found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a significantly higher gap between their chronological and biological ages than people born between 1950 and 1954. The younger the cohort examined, the wider that gap appeared to grow.

An investigation involving more than 10,000 US individuals revealed an even higher deviation for participants born between 1990 and 1999, compared to a cohort born between 1965 and 1969.

"In Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the US, people born in the 1990s face at least fourfold higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer compared with those in the 1960s," the authors write in the study.

Prostate cancer: The shift in early detection To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can I improve my biological age?

We used to assume that a healthy lifestyle could make up 75% to 90% of one's biological age. Now we know that's not true, Jachimowicz explains.

"We can influence about 50% of it," he says, "while the other 50% are genetically predetermined."

To help slow the aging process, he recommends "typical lifestyle interventions," such as working out regularly, eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, and avoiding drugs and alcohol.

And the value of social contacts should not be underestimated, he adds.

It's not easy to say why, on a biological level, younger generations are aging faster than their parents and grandparents. But there are a few hypotheses.

"Younger people are being exposed to earlier and longer obesity," says Tanwei Yuan, an epidemiologist in the Department of Clinical Epidemiology and Aging Research of the DKFZ in Heidelberg.

Other contributing factors are a sedentary lifestyle, and poor sleep quality due to extended periods of time in front of a screen, Yuan adds. She says the current study delivers valuable insights that confirm hypotheses long held by cancer researchers.

She also stresses the value of a healthy lifestyle to help reduce the risk of early-onset cancer.

"If you feel unwell, go to a doctor and ask for the screening," Yuan recommends.

Could microrobots be used to zap cancer cells? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yuan knows what she's talking about. The 32-year-old researcher says she had felt unwell for quite some time before being diagnosed with intestinal polyps last year. While these can start out benign, if left untreated, polyps can become cancerous. That's why it's important to listen closely to your body and take measures early, she says.

Can my doctor determine my biological age?

In a word: no, says Jachimowicz.

Determining an individual's biological age is the "subject of current scientific research, but in no way a practical routine or part of everyday clinical work."

However, he believes it should be, especially when it comes to initiating early cancer interventions. He believes this current study is particularly valuable because it highlights this path forward for future studies.

"It's still far off in the future," he says, "but it's very exciting."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Dry Danube River threatens nuclear power in Romania, Hungary
World.content:
Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant was operating at about 10% of capacity because of a lack of cooling riverwater. In Romania, the military blew up a rock outcrop in a bid to improve water flow to the Cernavoda plant.

Several central and eastern European countries are facing power shortages and impacts on industry amid prolonged hot and dry weather and record low levels on the Danube River and other waterways.

Hungary narrowly averted switching off its lone nuclear plant, but had still powered it down to a fraction of capacity. In Romania, the navy demolished a rocky outcrop exposed in the Danube's riverbed, trying to improve the water flow.

And in Serbia, hydroelectric power output was severely impacted by the dry conditions.

Continued hot and dry weather is forecast during the week, providing little sign of relief.

The Cernavoda nuclear plant draws its cooling water from the Danube Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

How did Romania try to feed the Cernavoda power plant?

Romania's military detonated a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels on a branch of the Danube, seeking to improve the flow of cooling water to the Cernavoda nuclear plant, which typically supplies about one-fifth of the country's power.

The plant draws all of its cooling water from the Danube.

Soldiers detonated a rock some 50 kilometers (roughly 30 miles) upstream. The debris would be taken to a strategic spot and sunk to help raise the water level.

Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the operation was a success, and also said the military had been waiting for a chance to access and demolish the rocks for decades.

Romania's navy was in action on the river on Monday Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

If the partial diversion of the water fails, Miruta said, the plant would likely have to shut down entirely by Thursday.

Caretaker Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan said that carmakers Dacia and Ford had agreed to suspend production in Romania until August 19, following a crisis meeting with representatives of the energy-intensive industry. He said that other companies would be taking similar steps.

What was the situation at Hungary's Paks power plant?

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said it was possible to avoid the unprecedented total shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant on Monday that was originally announced last week.

But the four-reactor station that typically generates almost half of Hungary's electricity production and around a third of its consumption was running at little more than 10% capacity on Monday.

The four-reactor Paks plant is a key contributor to Hungary's energy output Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO

Hungary had asked industrial users to curb consumption and households to make voluntary savings. Electric-powered freight trains were also stopped on Monday to reduce the load on the grid.

Magyar thanked people for their restraint on Monday evening.

"We have entered the critical period. The network is stable, consumption is currently well below planned levels, thanks to self-restraint. The last Paks turbine is operational. I will report back shortly from the (grid operator) MAVIR control room," he said.

Magyar also said slightly earlier on Monday that "water management forecasts for the coming days have become slightly more optimistic."

How power plant closure impacts Hungary's new government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How was Serbia affected?

In Serbia, the vast Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube was operating at only around one-fifth capacity on Monday.

Prime Miniser Djuro Macut convened an emergency meeting on Monday to discuss the energy problems.

He appealed to residents to "minimize the use of big consumers of electricity in their homes, such as air conditioners," having described the situation as "serious an demanding" late on Sunday.

Shallower stretches and Danube tributaries have been reduced to a trickle in the heat Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

Far upstream in Bavaria, the Danube's levels were also affecting freight transport.

New German Transport Minister Steffen Bilger said the historic low levels on the Danube, and particularly the Rhine to the west — Europe's busiest inland freight waterway — were providing a first challenge for his tenure.

"It is indeed a very tense situation with the low waters," Bilger told Reuters TV on Monday, saying he would chair a crisis meeting on Thursday. "We are used to repeated low water situations, but this is really a very early point in the calendar year for problems of the kind we're currently experiencing."

Typically European rivers reach their lowest levels slightly later in the summer — it's entirely possible that several more weeks of predominantly hot and dry weather are yet to come.

Danube water levels far upstream in Bavaria are also well below even their seasonal expectations Image: Manfred Segerer/IMAGO

World.title: Iran war: Trump tells Iranian leaders to make deal or surrender
World.content:
Skip next section Trump threatens Iran with 'decapitation' if no deal is reached

08/03/2026 August 3, 2026 Trump threatens Iran with 'decapitation' if no deal is reached

US President Donald Trump insisted that negotiations with Iran were ongoing, adding that the Islamic Republic was facing a "last chance before decapitation."

Trump told reporters at the White House that he agreed to continue to pursue talks with Iran at the request of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.

But Iran's foreign ministry has so far denied that negotiations with Washington were taking place.

"We are talking right now," Trump said.

"This is a last chance for them to sign a good document," the US president added. "I want to give them every last chance before decapitation."

The remarks were similar to last week's threat by Trump that Iran would be hit "very hard," facing potentially with renewed attacks against energy infrastructure. But the US president backed down later, saying the "perimeters" of a deal were there.

World.title: Ceuta: EU calls borders a 'shared European responsibility'
World.content:
The European Commission has offered Morocco more support at the border to Ceuta and Melilla, and called for "united action" from the bloc on border security. Its interior ministers will discuss the issue on Tuesday.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has told Spain's prime minister that border security is a "shared European responsibility" and suggested Brussels could provide more assistance to Morocco.

This comes as Spain tries to return the last of tens of thousands of people who swam around or otherwise breached the border to the North African exclave of Ceuta last week.

Officials installed an additional 500-meter barrier near the border post after thousands swam or waded around this entrance point Image: Jorge Guerrero/AFP

European Union interior ministers will convene for an emergency video meeting on Tueday to discuss potential responses. The scenes had led to friction betwen EU members and to Italy and France implementing temporary border controls, even though it's not possible to travel from Ceuta to the mainland without providing identification.

What did von der Leyen say in her letter to Spain's prime minister?

Von der Leyen wrote to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday, which was soon seen by several news agencies, calling for "united action" on border security within the bloc.

"From this incident it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points," she wrote.

"The protection of all our external borders is a shared European responsibility," von der Leyen said, calling for vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.

She commended Sanchez on his "swift handling" of the situation, with the vast majority of the roughly 50,000 people having already returned across the border to Morocco.

Ceuta's top government official Juan Jesus Vivas estimated that between 3,000 and 5,000 people remained in the city, with the Spanish governemnt's delegate offering a slightly lower estimate.

Von der Leyen also praised Morocco as an important security partner Image: Jon Nazca/REUTERS

Von der Leyen also raised the prospect of intensified cooperation with and assistance for Morocco if necessary when it came to the Spanish coastal exclaves of Ceuta and Melilla.

"Morocco is an important strategic partner, particularly in our efforts to combat migrant smuggling and illegal migration," von der Leyen wrote. "In cooperation with Spain, especially on anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.

Alone in Ceuta, 15-year-old Moroccan teen faces uncertainty To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

EU interior ministers' video conference set for Tuesday

The sudden large-scale rush across Ceuta's border starting on Thursday triggered sharp tensions among the EU's members states, with France announcing temporary border checks.

Migration-averse governments or ministers in Italy, Denmark and Finland even called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-travel area, while right-wing opposition politicians around the bloc were often even more vocal.

Madrid responeded critically to what it called a "selfish" response from some partners, and called for emergency talks among European interior minister to chart a way forward.

Von der Leyen said Tuesday's talks would be a "first step," promising the issue would also feature in October's EU leaders' summit.

What led to the rush into Ceuta, after months of reduced migration?

The EU has significantly tightened its migration rules in recent months, in steps that have led to a marked reduction in irregular migration into the bloc more generally.

It's also agreed on the option of sending failed asylum seekers to partner third countries deemed safe outside its borders, calling these destinations "return hubs." So far, though, no such deals have been set up even though legislation enabling them has been ushered in.

Migration expert Gerald Knaus, the director of the European Stability Initiative think tank, told DW it was clear that last week's developments were not based on "anything structural," given no meaningful changes either in Morocco's social situation or in Spain's migration policy.

Instead he said there "was a lot of false information" online wrongly spreading rumors like "Spain was opening its borders" and "there was an opportunity to get through."

He said the lower numbers of people swimming around the border checks earlier in the week fueled the fire and led to the vastly increased numbers by Thursday.

What did migration analyst Knaus say about the wider political response?

Knaus said the current situation was in no way comparable with the 2015 when thousands were arriving on a daily basis, many fleeing civil war in Syria.

"In this crisis, there were very, very few asylum seekers. Most of them were young Moroccan men. So, no, this is not a sudden increase in structural pressure from a big displacement crisis," he said.

But Knaus said that the political reaction throughout Europe and the way it generated similar panic and far-right calls to close the Schengen zone demonstrated that the difference in scale and the event being an outlier rather than a pattern didn't really matter.

"What we see is that politically, even two days of an event in North Africa create fear in Finland and Denmark and Germany," Knaus said. "And so clearly, all countries in Europe have an interest in helping the countries in the Mediterranean find a policy. And the policy has to be signaling clearly: Don't do this. Don't climb across the fence. Don't take to the boats. Don't swim across the sea. Because when you do, we will treat you humanely, but we will return you and if necessary, to a safe third country."

Knaus said that this message, if conveyed and shown to be true, would stop dangerous sea crossings almost completely and overnight. And he said that the new EU rules could make it possible to achieve.

However, he said he did not hold out much hope for the events in Ceuta leading to concerted action or cooperation among EU members.

"What is most likely is that there will be some grandstanding — that different governments will accuse each other. Spain will respond and will say it is not to blame and there will be bad feelings and no solution," Knaus predicted.

World.title: Growing impact of extreme heat on informal workers in Asia's cities
World.content:
When temperatures soar across Asia's cities, informal workers face a choice: risk their health or lose their income. For many, the effects don't end when the workday is over.

Brijpal Singh spends long hours working construction under the blazing sun in Noida, a sprawling industrial satellite city in India's National Capital Region. Even as temperatures soar past 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit), work on the building site rarely stops.

By the end of each shift, the 51-year-old says his heart is pounding, and he's usually dizzy, dehydrated and physically drained from hours in the heat. Yet taking a day off is a luxury he cannot afford.

Missing work would mean losing his daily wage of 500 to 600 rupees ($6 to $7, €5.20 to €6.10). The money supports his wife and three children living in a village in Uttar Pradesh, a two-day journey away .

"There are days when I don't feel like working," said Singh. "But if I miss a day, who will take care of my children and pay for their expenses?"

After a day in relentless heat on a construction site, Singh tries to find relief in front of a fan Image: Danish Pandit/DW

Some 5 million people work in the Delhi region's informal economy, accounting for roughly 80% of the total workforce. And as climate change drives up temperatures, many paid by the day like Singh are faced with an impossible trade-off between providing for their families and protecting their health.

Extreme heat harms health, productivity and earnings

The past decade has been India's warmest on record, bringing more frequent, intense, and prolonged heat waves. At the same time, heat is reducing productivity and increasing illnesses, with one study finding rising temperatures could be costing informal workers the equivalent of 2% of their country's GDP annually. That's nearly $80 billion (€69 billion).

"Wage losses are only going to worsen as temperatures continue to rise," said Ameena Kidwai, lead researcher at People's Courage International, a nonprofit aiming to strengthen informal workers' rights. "Workers are now putting in many more hours than they did before to complete the same amount of work."

The US-based organization surveyed informal workers in five Asian cities. Kidwai said some of those surveyed reported that tasks once completed in eight hours now take 10 to 12 hours during the hottest months, as they slow down to cope with dangerous conditions.

With heat becoming a major occupational hazard, workers described the harm to their health, ranging from respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses to stroke and kidney disease.

"As a result, workers also have to spend more on over-the-counter medicines and visits to clinics or hospitals," Kidwai said.

Out of the work frying pan and into the home furnace

A lack of ability to recover is a defining feature of urban heat for informal workers — from construction laborers and street vendors to delivery riders — say researchers.

Like Singh, many are migrants who leave their families behind to earn a living in fast-growing cities, said Patricia Samantha Narvaez, a program manager at the Philippine development organization IDEALS.

"You would expect home to be a place of relief," said Narvaez. "But many live in densely packed neighborhoods with poor ventilation, little green space and heat-absorbing concrete."

That's the case for Singh, who returns to a single room with poor ventilation after work. During the hot months from April to June, it becomes a furnace, and frequent power cuts make it difficult to cool down before the next day's shift.

"During the hot days, I can't eat well," Singh said. "I often drink oral rehydration solution and go to bed without eating."

Narvaez surveyed informal workers in Quezon City for a report on the impacts of extreme heat. The city is just northeast of Manila, the capital of the Philippines, a country in which some 42% of the employed population are informal workers.

"Some participants described Quezon City as a 'concrete jungle' because even at night it remains unbearably hot," said Narvaez.

Fifty-year-old Aida Tano has experienced such conditions firsthand. Tano worked in a garment factory in Quezon City for nearly two decades, where soaring temperatures, heat-generating machinery and poor ventilaton turned the production floor into an oven. With no air conditioning, four workers shared one electric fan.

Aida Tano, like many informal workers, bears the brunt of extreme heat both at her job and at home Image: People's Courage International

"There was no escape from the heat," Tano said. "We complained, but management told us that if we couldn't endure it, we could leave."

Narvaez says it's not unusual for factory owners to restrict measures that help workers cope with the heat even for trivial reasons such as not wanting fans to break down. At Tano's workplace, she had to pay for her own drinking water, and even climbing stairs to leave on her break became too exhausting in the heat.

The factory has since closed, but after a long day in extreme heat, Tano, who now does odd jobs like sewing and cleaning, would come back to a house with no AC. She still relies on electric fans and keeping windows covered to block the sun, both of which do little to cool her home.

Working women bear the brunt of extreme heat

The economic impacts of climate change hit women hardest, largely because they account for a majority of the world's poor, according to the United Nations.

Women in the informal economy also shoulder a disproportionately large burden because they combine paid work with unpaid caregiving responsibilities, said Ameena Kidwai of People's Courage International.

"They're managing their jobs while also running their households," Kidwai said. "When children or older family members fall sick during a heat wave, the caregiving duties falls largely on women."

Shanti Devi, a 36-year-old daily wage laborer in Noida, has been her family's sole breadwinner since her husband was injured in a workplace accident several years ago.

"Now I have to manage the house, care for my children and also try to earn a living," said Devi.

During heat waves, school closures and a shift to online classes often force Devi to stay home with her four children instead of going to work. Each day of lost wages adds to the already struggling family's financial strain.

"I took the day off because it is too hot to work, and my children are home because their school is closed for the summer," Devi said. "I have to cook for them. When school is open, they eat their meals there."

If Shanti Devi misses work to care for her children, she loses out on a much-needed pay check Image: Danish Pandi/DW

Frequent power outages and overheated homes, also leave many women up through the night caring for family members in the heat before returning to work the next day. Disrupted sleep and lack of rest come with increased health risks, such as heart disease and diabetes, meaning women are often more vulnerable than men in heat waves.

Researchers say these overlapping pressures expose a gap in many cities' efforts to adapt to a heating planet. While India has introduced heat action plans, and Quezon City is developing its own measures, protections for informal workers remain limited and unevenly enforced.

As temperatures rise because of human-caused climate change, experts say measures focus largely on short-term responses and often overlook the realities of informal workers' lives.

"Climate change will only deepen existing inequalities because those with the fewest resources are often the most exposed to extreme heat," Narvaez said. "Ultimately, resilient cities cannot be built on exhausted and unprotected workers."

Danish Pandit in Delhi, India, contributed to this report.

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

World.title: Russia says civilians killed in strike on Black Sea resort
World.content:
Moscow has accued Kyiv of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent weeks. Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy put Ukraine's chief peace negotiator in charge of foreign intelligence.

At least seven people, including three children, were killed in a Ukrainian strike on a Black Sea resort village of Arkhipo-Osipovka, authorities in Russia's Krasnodar region said on Monday.

Local governor Veniamin Kondratyev stated that falling drone debris injured at least 40 others, and accused Kyiv of attacking civilian targets far away from military installations.

It is unclear if the drone was intercepted before it landed on the beach. Ukraine has not yet commented on the strike.

Meanwhile, Sergey Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed governor of Crimea, said in a Telegram post that four people were killed in a Ukrainian strike on the Russia-annexed region.

Russian military officials said they have intercepted a further 131 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Kyiv did not confirm the strikes, but analysts said it was in line with the size of a recent spate of Ukrainian counter-attacks to Russian aggression.

At the same time, Ukraine said that an attack on a gas station in the Dnipropetrovsk had killed three people, in keeping with a recent pattern of Russian attacks on fuel depots.

This screenshot, taken from a video that was shared on social media, shows the moment when a drone collided with a beach Image: Social Media/REUTERS

Ukraine's negotiator to head foreign intelligence service

In the latest move in an ongoing shakeup in Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy appointed Rustem Umerov, Ukraine's chief peace negotiator, to lead foreign intelligence.

Zelenskyy said Umerov would remain in charge of peace talks after being moved from his previous job as head of the Security Council advisory body. Zelenskiy tasked Umerov with continuing to seek a diplomatic end to the war with Russia.

Ihor Klymenko, the former Interior Minister, will take over as head of the Security Council.

Since the sudden cabinet reshuffle last month, which included replacing Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, Zelenskyy has been shuffling senior officials among top posts. He has also replaced the top military commander, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

World.title: Binging on cringe: It's as addictive as 'eating junk food'
World.content:
Flexing achievements? Cringe. Expressing genuine emotions? Cringe. You want to look away, but you can’t. Cringe. It's so addictive, people have built social media careers by monetizing other people's worst moments.

I feel it. You probably do, too. Someone posts a crying selfie, proposes at a wedding, or confidently sings off-key at karaoke and we cringe.

We cringe when we see something so awkward, embarrassing, or painfully lacking in self-awareness that it makes us recoil.

But we're attracted to it at the same time because — perhaps — we've experienced similar situations ourselves or we know and care about people who have embarrassed themselves and we felt empathy.

And that's why cringe is also known in psychology as secondhand or vicarious embarrassment. We feel it on behalf of other people as well as their feeling it themselves. And sometimes we just enjoy watching other people suffer in a socially awkward situation.

Cringe has an online community: There are cringe compilations, reaction channels on cringe, comedy and other formats built on people's most cringeworthy moments. And people appear to be hooked.

Stefan Hofmann, a clinical psychologist specializing in social anxiety disorder at Marburg University, Germany, says cringe videos are as addictive as junk food: "If you eat junk food, you want more of it [or] even more outrageous stuff," Hofmann said.

Why we can't we look away from cringe moments

Embarrassment is subjective. A bad grade won't embarrass a person who doesn't care about school, but it can trigger real embarrassment in a person for whom academic success is central to their sense of self, their identity.

"If you see a complete stranger misbehaving in public, you might get angry," said Frieder Paulus, a psychologist and neuroscientist at the University of Lübeck, Germany.

"But if your kid is doing the same stuff, you might feel embarrassed, not only for the kid, but also for yourself," said Paulus, "because [you feel] the behavior of the kid reflects [on] you."

Virtual people: Why you can't always trust what you see To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Embarrassment belongs to a class of emotions called emotional barometers. Emotional barometers include shame, pride, and guilt. They signal a social norm has been broken.

For people to feel embarrassment, they have to be aware of the social norms, the context of the situation, and be aware there is an audience watching them.

Our reactions to embarrassing situations are visible on a brain scan.

"We see failure ... the arousal region [lights] up because something is not okay," said Paulus.

Why cringe is a useful reaction

Matthew Feinberg, a social psychologist at the University of Toronto in Canada, has found that people understand displays of embarrassment as a signal of prosocial behavior.

And that prosocial behavior creates a feeling of trust in the observer — they see that the person who is embarrassed knows they have done something socially awkward or wrong.

The message is: "I did something silly and I want to signal that it wasn't intentional and that I am a good member of society," said Feinberg.

On whether the same logic applies to the person observing someone else's mishap, Feinberg said witnessing embarrassment "triggers a natural response. My mind tells me to respond to that person with sympathy."

Feinberg said vicarious embarrassment may even be a stronger trust signal than being embarrassed yourself: "Possibly … because you're experiencing it even though you didn't do anything. It's an interesting research question that as far as I know hasn't been explored."

Millions followed her — then fake nudes appeared To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Exclusion: The cost of too much cringe

Embarrassment is also an expression of our fear that we may be excluded from a group when we do something embarrassing. For a social species such as that of humans and other animals, that can be dangerous.

"Fear of exclusion and fear of negative evaluation by others is painful psychologically as well as physically," said Hofmann. "It is certainly not the same quality of pain [as physical pain], but it's pain nonetheless."

In Hofmann's clinical work, he has tested so-called "social mishap exposures" in which patients embarrass themselves in an intentional and engineered way in an attempt to disprove the beliefs driving their fear or anxiety.

But cringe isn't something we can simply stop feeling. The emotion, researchers suggest, is involuntary and develops from an early age. And that also goes for associated emotions, such as empathy and trust, but also schadenfreude — not all of our addiction to cringe can be explained as an expression of positive emotion.

Hofmann says some people do experience pleasure when they see other people in embarrassing situations. And this distinction between empathy and schadenfreude also matters. If the pull toward cringe content was only about empathy, watching more of it would make us feel worse over time. But people keep watching cringe videos online.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

World.title: Can PM Modi reconnect with India's Gen Z?
World.content:
Student protests exposed a growing disconnect between PM Narendra Modi's BJP and young Indians. Experts say Instagram reels alone won't close it.

As students filled India's streets to demand accountability from the government, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi seemed to have realized that he needed to connect more effectively with the country's youth.

Modi posted on Instagram a rare selfie video in which he said he was pained by their suffering and promised remedial steps. But it was not enough to satisfy the protesters' concerns, and five Gen Z-style reels later, that gap seems as wide as ever.

"We ain't friends," one comment under the first reel read. It echoed thousands of others reacting to a midnight video drop from the PM.

In one of Modi's lesser-produced videos, he addressed the youth as "friends" before finally speaking about the exam at the center of the protests.

It was the prime minister’s response to the biggest political crisis he has faced in his third term so far, over a cancelled high-stakes medical entrance exam which affected millions of aspirants.

Since the first video, he's improved camera angles and lighting, tried varied backgrounds, and even started and ended the videos himself like a one-man content creator. The response remains tepid.

For Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the protests came at the peak of its power, but the unrest has dimmed that shine, and the disconnect with the youth is substantial, experts told DW.

Young voices sidelined

In 2024, the average age of MPs elected to India's Parliament reached a record 56 years, which is a problem, said Shipra Baduni, CEO of Young Leaders for Active Citizenship, because there is not much youth representation in the legislature.

The second shift is in the nation's youth politics.

India has traditionally had vibrant youth participation at the university level, where student parties have long been affiliated with national and regional parties.

"Student politics has not only given a pulse check, or given a platform for young people to be able to express frustration, or anger, or dissent," said Baduni. "It's also given some of these parties and leaders today."

"We've seen systematically over the last one decade that it has been cut down," she added. "There is a very evident push to say that students should only study, and there is no need for students to engage in politics."

"Where is the space for a young person to express their frustration? If you go on social media to criticize the government, there is a crackdown. Offices are screening your social media."

But Baduni believes the responsibility to connect with the youth doesn't lie with the central government alone: "It's the job of my ward councillor or my local elected leader to come out and say, 'let me talk to the young people in my locality, what are your concerns?'."

DW reached out to BJP's youth leader for New Delhi and the party's national spokesperson, but did not receive a response from either.

Decoding the Gen Z vibe

Memes and music formed the backbone of reels posted on social media, while some young adults politely made their demands and others used expletives in sing-song slogans.

When the government responded, that response itself became fodder for a new wave of memes and content.

"The BJP does not understand expression of anger through ironic humor/memes, because their strategy was focused on the WhatsApp generation," political scientist and author Amit Julka told DW.

"Even now, let's say the BJP's PR department were to say we are now going to crack the Gen Z code, the result will be fundamentally inorganic."

Over a week after the protests were called off following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the national conversation has shifted — not to education reform and preventing paper leaks, but to "misguided youths."

Delhi police crack down on student protests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Several BJP members and supporters posted messages saying the abuses were against Indian moral codes and had deeply unsettled them. They were referring to a viral video where a teenage girl used abusive language against the Prime Minister and his late mother.

In a reel posted over the weekend, Modi addressed the teenager's words.

"I can fully understand the outrage within society. It comes as a cultural shock to see our daughters using such language," Modi said, adding that he wanted to "forgive them" rather than see them dragged through court proceedings.

Modi's senior ministerial colleague Rajnath Singh said last weekend that the government's "top priority remains to understand our students' genuine concerns, ​address them promptly, and ensure that they know their voices are being heard."

Julka pointed to this episode as one way the BJP can delegitimize dissenters going forward. "There doesn't necessarily need to be an application of coercion. Sometimes even a veiled allusion is enough," he said, adding that Gen Zs were ultimately "vulnerable" youth.

What can bridge the political gap?

Working at the cross-section of youth and policy, Baduni believes the BJP still has non-coercive ways to bridge the gap. First, by staying on topic.

"The agenda of the protest is the systematic failure of the education system in India that has failed so many people. Why are you, even today, not talking about that?" she asked.

Baduni suggested that the BJP government needs to speak with the youth at various civic levels and make constructive changes while refraining from further crackdowns.

"I'm not sure how much of it is going to reverse the dent that has already been made," she said, adding that it could give the BJP a better sense of the issues that matter to young people and help the party begin addressing them.

"If you tell them that they will only be heard if they're disruptive, then there is no incentive for them to not be disruptive," Baduni noted.

Education minister concedes to 'Cockroach' demands, resigns To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the protests against the education minister ended, several smaller demonstrations have been reported across India.

In Uttar Pradesh's Fatehpur, hundreds of students staged a peaceful walkout to bring the district's attention to infrastructure gaps. In a government school in western India, students protested to demand more teachers. In Jaipur, three student leaders began an indefinite hunger strike, demanding restoration of student union elections.

As for Modi's series of reels, both Baduni and Julka said the one-sided interaction wasn't a real solution.

"That will just give Gen Z a lot more content on what's wrong with this government," said Baduni.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: “En el rap, destaca el que tiene más ingenio. Lo que hacemos tiene un verdadero peso cultural”
World.content:
Arkano, el adolescente que descubrió su identidad gracias al rap. Conversaciones sobre la educación que queremos | Pensemos el mañana (Episodio 2)

Arkano, rapero y referente del ‘freestyle’ en España, se sienta a conversar con Bohemia, una joven promesa de la improvisación, sobre cómo el error forma parte del aprendizaje, cómo gestionar las críticas y cómo la educación colabora en crear mejores artistas urbanos

Guillermo Rodríguez 'Arkano' Artista de rap Su trayectoria reúne algunos de los grandes hitos del freestyle desde que, con 15 años, se proclamó campeón de España de la Red Bull Batalla de los Gallos de 2009. Incluso batió un récord Guinness al improvisar durante 24 horas y 34 minutos seguidos. Paralelamente, impulsa y participa en iniciativas sobre salud mental y colabora en campañas contra el acoso escolar Isabel Arrabal 'Bohemia' Estudiante de 3º de ESO Y ‘freestyler’ A sus 15 años, compagina los estudios en el IES Averroes (Córdoba) con sus primeras competiciones de freestyle. Empezó a improvisar con 14 años, tras descubrir el rap en YouTube, y forma parte de una nueva generación de jóvenes que ha encontrado en la cultura urbana un lugar donde desarrollar su confianza

Dice Arkano (Alicante, 32 años) que el rap le transformó, que incluso le salvó la vida. A los 15 años, cuando aún lo conocían más como Guillermo Rodríguez y todavía cursaba la ESO, ganó en España la Red Bull Batalla de los Gallos, la competición de improvisación más importante del país. “Yo era un chaval muy tímido, no tenía habilidades sociales, lo pasé bastante mal en la época del instituto y descubrir el rap fue como encontrar una voz propia”, cuenta. La cultura urbana le alumbró, le infundió más confianza.

“El 'freestyle' se basa en lanzarse al vacío, no podemos aspirar a que todo sea perfecto. Tenemos que estar preparados para el error”

Isabel Arrabal, conocida como Bohemia, tiene la misma edad que tenía Arkano cuando se coronó como una joven promesa. No es su única coincidencia; esta cordobesa también ha ganado seguridad en sí misma después de atreverse a rapear. En Pensemos el mañana, el proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y Grupo Prisa sobre la educación del futuro, reflexionan sobre cómo han podido desarrollarse gracias a sus inquietudes artísticas y a esos entornos sociales fuera de las aulas, no convencionales.

"El rap me ayudó mucho a relacionarme con mis compañeros, a tener más seguridad en lo que hago, porque antes era muy tímida. Me ha ayudado a confiar más en mí”

Bohemia y Arkano charlan, además, sobre lograr que el miedo a equivocarse no les inmovilice, la relación entre educación y rap (y la importancia de tener “un lenguaje más rico”, como precisa Arkano) o la gestión de críticas y redes sociales. Aunque sea una asignatura pendiente para algunos adolescentes, Bohemia ha aprendido a manejar esos mensajes anónimos y ofensivos: “A mucha gente le puede llegar a afectar, y el consejo que les daría es que piensen en quiénes son ellos realmente”.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

World.title: CGT mantiene la huelga de servicios en tierra en el aeropuerto de Barcelona desde mañana
World.content:
El paro afectará al personal de asistencia, facturación y embarque de pasajeros y coordinación de vuelos del aeropuerto

La sección sindical de CGT en Groundforce, sociedad del grupo Globalia que presta servicios en tierra (‘handling’) en el Aeropuerto de Barcelona-El Prat, mantiene la huelga indefinida que ha convocado a partir de este martes 4 de agosto a las 00:00 horas. El paro afectará al personal de asistencia en tierra, facturación y embarque de pasajeros y coordinación de vuelos del aeropuerto — formadopor 1.179 trabajadores —, según ha informado este lunes en un comunicado el sindicato, que cuenta con mayoría en el comité de empresa de la compañía, integrado por 27 delegados.

La decisión, según este sindicato, responde a la inacción de la dirección ante el “grave deterioro” de la prevención de riesgos y las condiciones de salud laboral en la base. La portavoz de CGT, Esther García, ha afirmado que están a la espera de que la empresa se siente a hablar con ellos, pero de momento continúan con la protesta ante una situación “en la que la plantilla ya no puede más”, con sobrecarga de trabajo y falta de formación para las contrataciones nuevas.

En marzo, CCOO, UGT y USO convocaron una huelga indefinida en la misma compañía, que presta servicio de asistencia en tierra en los aeropuertos de Barcelona, Madrid, Alicante, Valencia, Palma, Ibiza, Málaga, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Tenerife, Lanzarote, Fuerteventura y Bilbao.

11.600 vuelos y 2 millones de pasajeros posibles afectados

Groundforce obtuvo 12 licencias en la última adjudicación para el servicio de asistencia en tierra de Aena, en septiembre de 2023, para los doce aeropuertos de mayor volumen de carga en los que opera la compañía en España.

Actualmente, Groundforce atiende a aerolíneas internacionales y nacionales que operan en ambas terminales del aeropuerto barcelonés, como Air Europa, Lufthansa, Air France, KLM, Qatar Airways, ElAl, Etihad Airways, SAS, Air Arabia, Turkish Airlines, ITA Airways, LOT Polish Airlines, Croatia Airlines, United Airlines, Finnair, Asiana Airlines, Saudia Airlines, Air China, Air Transat o Luxair.

Está previsto que, desde el inicio de la huelga, mañana día 4, y hasta el mes de septiembre, las compañías atendidas por Groundforce en Barcelona programen unos 11.600 movimientos, ofertándose cerca de 2,4 millones de asientos.

Según el Ministerio de Transporte y Movilidad Sostenible, atendiendo a los factores de ocupación previstos para estos meses, se podrían ver afectados cerca de 2 millones de pasajeros.

Servicios mínimos

Según la resolución del ministerio, para la operativa comercial ha fijado una protección del 80 % en agosto y del 77 % en septiembre para las conexiones del Aeropuerto de Barcelona con territorios no peninsulares o bajo obligación de servicio público.

En el caso de las rutas internacionales y los vuelos peninsulares cuya alternativa de transporte público supere las cinco horas, los servicios mínimos serán del 58 % en agosto y del 57 % en septiembre. Por su parte, las rutas peninsulares con una alternativa de transporte inferior a cinco horas tendrán garantizada una operativa del 35 % durante el mes de agosto y del 36 % en septiembre.

World.title: Las Bolsas europeas conquistan nuevos máximos y el Ibex roza los 20.000 puntos
World.content:
La moderación del precio del petróleo y el impulso de los resultados empresariales permiten al Ibex acariciar los 20.000 puntos. El selectivo español ha repuntado un 1,01% en la primera jornada de agosto y se ha quedado a tan solo 17 puntos de conseguir semejante hazaña. A falta de superar ese nivel psicológico, el cierre de este lunes es suficiente para alcanzar nuevas cotas históricas (durante la jornada ha llegado a situarse en los 19.987 puntos) y subirse a la ola de máximos históricos de la que disfruta la renta variable europea, con el Stoxx 600, el Dax alemán y el Cac francés batiendo sus propios récords.

Si la Bolsa española se enfrentó a una travesía en el desierto de 18 años, con su propia crisis financiera, una pandemia mundial y un shock inflacionista para lograr superar los máximos alcanzados en 2007, en los últimos 10 meses el Ibex ha logrado revalidar sus récords y alcanzar niveles hasta el momento inexplorados. Lo ha logrado gracias a un sector, castigado tiempo atrás, como es la banca, y pese a no poder subirse al fervor de la inteligencia artificial, debido al escaso peso de las empresas tecnológicas en la Bolsa española.

La moderación del precio del petróleo está jugando a favor de la renta variable. La decisión del presidente estadounidense Donald Trump de pausar los ataques en Oriente Próximo para dar una oportunidad a la negociación ha sido un alivio para el crudo. El barril de brent baja un 7%, hasta los 83,8 dólares. Los analistas de GVC Gaesco reconocen que la cercanía de los índices europeos a zona de máximos “invita a mantener cierta cautela”. “No se perciben señales de euforia desmedida, pero sí una dependencia creciente de que el contexto geopolítico continúe estabilizándose y de que los bancos centrales dispongan de espacio para suavizar su mensaje en los próximos meses”, añaden.

Trump aseguró el domingo que había cancelado la ofensiva prevista contra Irán tras recibir una solicitud de Teherán y otros países de Oriente Próximo para avanzar en las negociaciones. “Nos han pedido que suspendamos cualquier ataque, ya que se han acordado los términos de un acuerdo”, afirmó el mandatario en una publicación en la red social Truth Social. Añadió que el acuerdo propuesto incluiría la “APERTURA INMEDIATA, COMPLETA Y TOTAL DEL ESTRECHO DE ORMUZ, y el fin de la amenaza nuclear de Irán”.

La respuesta de Teherán ha sido una nueva negativa. “Actualmente, no estamos negociando con Estados Unidos. Nuestras negociaciones con Omán se centran en llegar a un acuerdo sobre una ruta que permita reanudar el paso seguro de los buques por el estrecho de Ormuz”, ha asegurado el portavoz del Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores de Irán, Esmaeil Baghaei. El régimen iraní está, según ha aclarado, trabajando con Omán para permitir que el tráfico marítimo por el estrecho de Ormuz atraviese una nueva ruta “temporal” que permita una mayor circulación de embarcaciones y que evite zonas que hayan podido ser minadas.

A pesar de los posibles cantos de sirena, los analistas de UBS advierten de los peligros. “Está por ver si finalmente se alcanza un acuerdo y si el estrecho se reabrirá rápidamente, pero seguimos creyendo que el principal motor de las acciones será el sólido crecimiento de los beneficios empresariales”. En opinión de sus estrategas, “el ciclo de inversión en inteligencia artificial continúa intacto a corto plazo y que una política monetaria estable de la Reserva Federal seguirá respaldando al mercado, mientras que la resiliencia de la economía estadounidense sostiene una subida más amplia y diversificada de las Bolsas. Con el crecimiento del beneficio por acción del S&P 500 en el segundo trimestre encaminado a alcanzar o superar el 30%, creemos que existe margen para nuevas alzas en la renta variable estadounidense”.

La atención de los inversores se centra ahora en determinar si los catalizadores que impulsaron el repunte reciente de las acciones pueden seguir generando subidas. Si bien las grandes empresas tecnológicas han cumplido en gran medida con las expectativas de ganancias del mercado, los inversores están cada vez más inquietos por el creciente gasto relacionado con la IA, sin que de momento haya pruebas evidentes de que genere los retornos esperados para justificar esas enormes inversiones. “La principal conclusión que saqué de esos resultados financieros de las empresas tecnológicas es que los inversores no tienen ganas de seguir pagando y pagando sin tener una idea clara de lo que este gasto de capital va a generar en términos de ganancias”, dijo Megan Horneman, directora de inversiones de Verdence Capital Advisors, en declaraciones a la CNBC.

Por lo pronto, el mercado se prepara para jornadas de elevada volatilidad. Michiel Tukker, estratega senior de tipos para Reino Unido y la zona euro de ING, comenta que “los mercados tienen que asimilar una gran cantidad de datos macroeconómicos y declaraciones de los bancos centrales de la semana pasada, y con la publicación de las cifras de empleo estadounidenses prevista para el viernes, se espera una mayor volatilidad”.

El mercado permanece atento a las divisas, después de que Japón y Estados Unidos decidieran intervenir en el mercado para frenar el castigo al yen. Una intervención conjunta, la primera en 30 años, que puede ser el inicio de nuevas operaciones, según ha avanzado el ejecutivo nipón, y con la que aspira a frenar su depreciación frente al dólar después de que el yen alcanzara mínimos de cuatro décadas frente a la divisa estadounidense.

Mientras tanto, en el mercado de deuda, los inversores han levantado el castigo a la deuda estadounidense visto días atrás. Pese a la amenaza de una inflación persistente aún latente y un poso de falta de credibilidad en la Reserva Federal tras las palabras utilizadas por el presidente de la institución, Kevin Warsh, la rentabilidad del bono a 30 años ha bajado al 5,226%, y la del bono con vencimiento a una década se modera hasta el 4,692%.
