World.title: Melbourne public hospital doctors to strike next week
World.content:
Victorian doctors will walk off the job next week at some of the state's busiest hospitals as part of a pay dispute with the state government.

It will be the first protected industrial action at Victorian public hospitals for 20 years.

The Australian Medical Association Victoria (AMAV) said public hospital doctors will stop work at hospitals in Parkville and Melbourne's CBD for several hours on August 13.

The work ban, involving members of the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation, will run from 12:30pm until 4pm and workers will rally in Grattan Street in the city.

Hospitals affected include the Royal Melbourne Hospital, the Royal Children's Hospital and the Royal Women's Hospital as well as other facilities.

AMAV said affected hospitals have been asked to reschedule non-life-threatening appointments on that day.

The Victorian branch of the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation is set to take industrial action ahead of the November state election. (Unsplash: Frederick Medina)

It is understood doctors in emergency departments and other critical frontline services will not take part in the work ban.

AMAV president Simon Jenkins said doctors had tried to negotiate a better deal with the government over pay and conditions for 12 months.

"Up to 50 per cent of, particularly our doctors in training, report incredibly high levels of fatigue and stress, and they're incredibly worried in those conditions about whether they might be prone to making errors," he said.

"Many of our doctors still don't get paid for overtime, a lot of our consultants are on call after hours and don't get paid for overtime.

"We're also looking at shifts, shift fatigue, making sure doctors get adequate breaks when they're on work."

AMAV said 97 per cent of union members voted in favour of the protected industrial action.

In addition to the work bans at the major Melbourne public hospitals, doctors will also begin other statewide actions, such as disrupting billing of patients and refusing to do unscheduled overtime.

Doctors will also refuse to answer emails and phone calls from hospital management.

World.title: With a new heart, 18-month-old Noah is finally coming home
World.content:
After enduring the unimaginable, the Forster family are set for an emotional cross-country journey home to Western Australia.

Their 18-month-old son Noah has had a successful heart transplant, surviving the condition that claimed the life of his older brother Teddy.

Little Noah is ready to come home to Busselton in WA after a successful heart transplant. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

Sinead and Alex Forster's second son was just six days old when he was diagnosed with ventricular non-compaction dilated cardiomyopathy, affecting his heart's left ventricle.

Teddy, the couple's firstborn son, died waiting for a transplant at 20 months old.

"We didn't want the fear of what had happened to Teddy to stop us from trying again," Ms Forster said.

Ms Forster said the young family moved to Melbourne for medical care soon after Noah was diagnosed.

It was a decision that saved his life, his mother said.

"They wanted to get Noah in a place that could give him the best possible support before he got very, very sick," Ms Forster said.

Noah Forster will make a road trip home, with the family opting to drive as his immune system recovers. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

Call 'we never thought would come'

Noah went into heart failure at seven months old, and was kept alive by a ventricular assist device.

After nine long months, the family received the call that a suitable donor had been found.

"You're waiting for this phone call that you never thought will come," Ms Forster said.

" To receive that call and to be told that your child has a chance at a life, and you can move on from this limbo that you've been living in, takes your breath away. "

Joy after tragedy

For the Forsters, the memory of their first son Teddy is ever present.

"[Noah has] always got his big brother Teddy watching over him so he can accomplish anything," Ms Forster said.

Noah was their "rainbow baby", their chance for a family after the devastating loss of Teddy, she explained.

The Forsters tragically lost their first-born, Teddy, to heart complications. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

Ms Forster said cardiologists had told the couple they had a one-in-two chance of having another child with a similar condition.

"We thought, let's take the chance, let's try and have a family," she said.

"Being pregnant with another child and not knowing the future was very scary.

"After such a long time of waiting and then still losing Teddy, this baby was going to be our second chance."

Teddy died while waiting for a donor heart. (Supplied: Sinead Forster)

The Forsters are also painfully aware, as they celebrated the life of their second son, that the family of their donor was grieving.

"We will forever be thankful for that family, and for that child for this amazing gift that they've given our son," she said.

" They've really given him a chance at life. Not even a second chance. This is a chance at life. "

Family's courage praised

Heart Kids regional family support coordinator Ariana Potts met the Forsters after the birth of their first son Teddy.

"They are the most compassionate and generous family and they have shown immense courage," she said.

Ms Potts said the experience could be incredibly isolating, and creating a support network is very important.

"It's an incredibly difficult time for all the families and I think they need as much support as possible," Ms Forster said.

Organ donor opt-out A proposal to automatically make people organ donors could reduce the number of available organs.

Long trip home

Noah, now recovering from the surgery, is ready to return home.

The family is choosing to drive, in a bid to protect his vulnerable immune system.

The drive is also a chance for the family to make lasting memories.

"Putting an 18-month-old on a plane, where we can't get him to wear a mask, we can't protect him from the germs around us," Ms Forster said.

"This will be our last chance together before normal life begins."

Noah had shown resilience, with a smile on his face, throughout the ordeal.

World.title: How a father's love of music took his daughter to the world stage
World.content:
How do you raise a musical child?

What if she becomes more famous than you?

For baritone Christopher Allan and his daughter, soprano Miriam Allan, a love of music matters more than success or fame.

Christopher Allan raised his family in Newcastle, NSW. When Miriam grew up, her career took her to the UK, where she is now raising her own family in the town of Windsor.

At the height of the COVID-19 lockdowns, Miriam Allan attracted international attention as the soprano in the four-person choir that accompanied Prince Philip's scaled-back funeral at St George's Chapel, Windsor.

Her father watched proudly from his home in Newcastle.

Despite living on opposite sides of the world, Christopher and Miriam Allan share a close bond built on their love of music and music education.

Miriam and Christopher Allan last appeared onstage together in Newcastle in 2019. (Supplied: Photolook Newcastle)

Now, they're preparing to tour J.S. Bach's Coffee Cantata, showing the composer's lighter side through the story of a father trying (and failing) to stop his daughter from drinking too much coffee.

We talk with Christopher and Miriam Allan about their family's love of music, navigating life across continents, and why each considers the other their favourite performing partner.

On raising a musical child …

Christopher: Music was always around.

I've got photos of Mim [Miriam] in her bassinet underneath the harpsichord while we were rehearsing.

She started piano lessons at five, and we soon realised she has perfect pitch.

She joined the Cathedral choir in Newcastle when she turned six.

By the time she was 18, she'd already sung on the ABC, and done some professional gigs with the Song Company.

I was teaching at Newcastle Conservatorium when Miriam decided to study music.

We had to arrange for her to be taught by a teacher from another university.

Otherwise, it would've been impossible to assess her.

On having a musical parent …

Miriam: I have so many memories of sitting down at the piano and playing with Dad when I was a little kid.

Miriam Allan has fond memories of her dad, Christopher Allan, playing the piano when she was growing up. (ABC Newcastle: Sofie Wainwright)

I remember seeing Dad sing on major stages, including the Sydney Opera House, when I was a teenager.

And Dad was involved in a huge number of education projects where he would get kids singing in any way, shape or form.

He showed me how to make music, how to make it big, and how to make it accessible.

Without that role modelling, I genuinely wouldn't be doing what I'm doing now. And I don't think a number of kids who grew up in Newcastle would be either.

On singing at Prince Philip's funeral …

Miriam: When the Duke of Edinburgh passed away, there were COVID protocols regarding social distancing, including allowing only three singers to perform at one time.

For the funeral, it was decided at the highest levels of government that they could indeed have four singers.

And so, the Director of Music, who at the time lived in a house behind mine, came round and spoke to me through the window and asked if I would do the service.

I'd been sworn to secrecy, but I said to the powers that be, "Is it possible I could just let my dad know?"

Christopher: It was huge for me to watch Miriam, for a whole lot of reasons.

Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip were important figures in Christopher Allan's household. (ABC Newcastle: Sofie Wainwright)

I emigrated here from England at the age of seven. So, it's interesting to me that Mim has gone back and lived there when my parents came to Australia to give my siblings and me a better life.

The Queen and Prince Philip were very important figures in our house.

It's that kind of level of pride and enjoyment, and just the sheer thought of "we're from Newcastle; things like this don't happen."

For Miriam to take part in that was a huge honour for her.

On keeping musically connected across continents

Miriam: We do talk a lot, especially about music and music education, because I'm a music educator too. We send each other articles that we read or things that we find interesting, and we talk about students a lot.

Christopher: Until COVID put a dent in things, we'd see each other every 18 months or so.

Miriam: It's not uncommon, when I come back to Australia or when Dad comes to the UK, for me to sit poor old Dad at a piano, hand him a whole stack of music, and say: "Off we go."

On being father and daughter on stage …

Christopher: If any of my children wanted to do something and their mother had said no, they would say, "It always works with Daddy."

In the Bach cantata we'll be performing, there's a conversation where the father tells his daughter to give up drinking so much coffee, and the daughter says, "I'm not giving up my coffee."

And I can just hear my own children as teenagers going, "Yeah, whatever. We're going to do what we want anyway because it always works with Daddy."

Miriam: Coffee is the subject of this cantata, but the disagreement between father and daughter could be replaced with just about anything.

But the hilarious thing is that Dad loves coffee and I cannot stand the stuff.

I do love a cup of tea, though. So, if anyone out there wants to bring me a cuppa, I probably won't say no.

This interview has been edited for clarity.

Christopher and Miriam Allan will be performing with Bach Akademie Australia from August 5–16 in Brisbane, Newcastle, Sydney, Canberra and Glenbrook.

World.title: Hens moved indoors but free-range label still allowed
World.content:
The consumer watchdog has extended its pause on free-range egg labelling enforcement, as some farmers move hens indoors to protect them from H5 bird flu on state government advice.

Usually eggs can only be labelled as free range if producers meet several requirements for hens, including access to outdoors and stocking densities of no more than 10,000 hens per hectare.

As bird flu cases continue to rise, the Australian Consumer and Competition Commission (ACCC) is allowing farmers to keep chickens indoors and still use free-range cartons.

Under law, eggs labelled free range usually have to come from hens able to roam and forage outdoors. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

But ACCC deputy chair, Mick Keogh, said producers needed to let consumers know what's going on.

"If they've got their birds housed, there's an obligation to communicate that, particularly to retailers, but also more widely, to the consumers," he said.

Poultry still free of H5

H5 hasn't spread to poultry or the agriculture industry in Australia yet, but Mr Keogh said the risk was increasing.

"The spread in wild bird populations is continuing to grow … that suggests to us that the threat or the risk for domestic poultry, in particular, is growing," he said.

In early July, the ACCC confirmed it would not take enforcement action for breaches of free-range egg labelling standards, as voluntary housing measures started.

Mr Keogh said that would continue, for now.

"We don't see the situation has changed; in fact, if anything, [it] has become more urgent."

No timeframe has been set for an end to the enforcement pause.

Zac Jeffries and his wife Alana would like temporary labels to be used on cartons. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

Pasture-raised egg farm, Providore Farm, sits on the outskirts of Portland, in south-west Victoria, near where several infected greater crested terns were found.

Owner Zac Jeffries said he did not have an indoor option for his birds at the moment, and he was concerned about misleading egg labelling.

"I definitely don't like the idea that someone can be marketing their eggs as free range when they're not actually living like that," he said.

He wants to see temporary label changes, allowing farmers to use the same cartons.

"There's a two to three month wait to get a carton in … and when we do a minimum order, it's 60,000 cartons.

"It really wouldn't be hard to have a sticker or something that we applied to our carton saying, 'Temporarily inside due to government order' or 'during this outbreak.'"

Mr Jeffries said bigger farms should be able to make necessary changes.

"I don't think they should be able to continue just pumping out cartons of eggs, calling them free range when the birds are locked in for two or three months at a time."

State governments have made voluntary orders urging poultry farmers to protect flocks from infection. (Supplied: Providore Farm)

Mr Keogh acknowledged the enforcement pause may be confusing for consumers and farmers alike.

"Consumers do want to trust what they're being told and make sure it's right," he said.

"We [also] acknowledge completely that to get a box run of some thousands of egg cartons and get the labels changed is a very expensive thing."

But he said the longer the outbreak continued, it was important that free-range producers "make efforts to communicate the reality of the situation".

"Advising retailers, for example, that they may want to put signs on the shelf saying, 'In the current situation, some of these birds may have been kept in housing, and it may not be free range,'" Mr Keogh said.

Mick Keogh says free range egg farmers need to let consumers know if their hens are kept inside. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Mandatory orders on table

Voluntary housing orders are in place in several states, including in South Australia, where the bulk of the country's confirmed H5 cases are.

SA's chief vet, Dr Skye Fruean, said it was a "very dynamic situation and we are remaining really closely engaged with our poultry sector."

She said a mandatory housing order was not in place yet, but was being considered.

"It is an option open to jurisdictions at the end of the day to make their own decisions," she said.

Once state authorities declare mandatory orders for egg and chicken meat farmers to keep birds indoors, the ACCC's enforcement pause is limited to 90 days.

World.title: Haugset goes it alone to claim Tour de France Femmes third stage
World.content:
Sigrid Haugset has set off on a long solo run and kept going to the finish to win the third stage of the Women's Tour de France and claim the yellow jersey.

The Norwegian rider made her break with more than half of the tough 156.5-kilometre route between Geneva and Poligny to go.

The stage featured four categorised climbs and Haugset made her move with 85 kilometres left, at the foot of the category two Col de la Savine.

Haugset was also first across the last listed climb of the day, the category four Côte de Chaux-Champagny, followed by Lotte Kopecky about 30 seconds behind, and a nine-rider group more than two minutes adrift.

Previous yellow jersey holder Lorena Wiebes, who won the first two stages, was 13 minutes behind with the main bunch at the time. She ultimately finished more than 20 minutes adrift of Haugset and dropped to 67th in the general classification.

It was a battle between two riders going into the last 10 kilometres. Kopecky had cut Haugset's lead to 15 seconds and the Belgian rider could just about see her rival ahead.

But Haugset, sensing the danger, stood on her pedals to stay ahead and managed to increase her lead again, finishing 1:24 ahead of Kopecky.

Haugset leads the general classification by 2:02 from Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius, with 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering third, a further four seconds behind.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women's Tour, covers 1,175 kilometres over nine days.

World.title: 12yo relies on blood donors to keep her alive, but there's a big shortage
World.content:
Australian Red Cross Lifeblood says more than 12,000 donors are needed over the next seven days as the nation faces ongoing shortages of type O and A blood.

The organisation said the peak winter flu season had kept donors away because they needed to be clear of respiratory symptoms for seven days before they could donate.

Donated blood is essential for people like 12-year-old Yasmin Sayed, who has a blood disorder called sickle cell thalassaemia.

"My blood cells die quicker because they're not formed properly, so I'll die without getting blood," she said.

Yasmin says she would die without blood transfusions. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

She had her first blood transfusion at six months old, and needs a transfusion every four weeks at the Sydney Children's Hospital in Randwick.

"I'm kind of used to it now, it's like a second home," she said.

Her father, Rabih Sayed, said he was eternally grateful to blood donors.

"My family wouldn't be the family it is today without these people and their generosity," he said.

"We can see her grow, get bigger and that sort of stuff. Without the donations we'd be missing part of our family."

Impact of late cold and flu peak

Lifeblood area manager for Sydney, John Bain, said up to 1,600 appointments were sitting empty every day, with many people cancelling or rescheduling appointments due to winter illnesses.

"The cold and flu peak this year has come a little later, so we are into August now, but we are aware lots of people certainly in the last couple of weeks to a month have been cut down with it and it's definitely showing in our bookings," he said.

Mr Bain says winter illnesses have prompted many people to cancel their appointments to donate blood. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Even mild symptoms such as sniffles, sore throats, and headaches make people temporarily ineligible to give blood.

Richard Mitchell, who is an oncologist at the Sydney Children's Hospital, was among those rolling up his sleeve at Lifeblood's Moore Park donor centre this week.

He said many of his patients needed regular transfusions and he was concerned about the dip in available donors during winter.

"Blood transfusions are a life-essential part of what we do every day," Dr Mitchell said.

" We use red blood cells, we use platelets, we use plasma, we use proteins for the immune system. All of these things are lifesaving therapies to make sure the kids can survive. "

Dr Mitchell says many of his patients need regular blood transfusions. (ABC News: Adam Griffiths)

Most demand in Victoria

Lifeblood said recent appeals had prevented supplies from falling to critical levels, but they had not been enough to replenish low stocks of O-positive and O-negative, the blood types most commonly used in emergencies.

A-positive blood stocks have also dropped in recent weeks.

"We are well below where we would like to be to be sitting comfortably to fill all of our orders," Mr Bain said.

Victoria is currently the state with the highest demand, with 4,500 donors needed, while NSW needs 3,100 and Queensland 3,000.

Mr Bain said it only takes an hour of a donor's time.

"The actual blood donation in itself only takes eight to 10 minutes and you get some great snacks and a relax at the end," he said.

"Honestly, you feel fantastic. It's that pride of helping a stranger. It's that feeling of fulfilment."

World.title: Farmer sends $40k bill to Victorian government for dingo attacks on sheep
World.content:
A north-west Victorian farmer driven to his wit's end by wild dogs killing his sheep has invoiced the state government for the losses.

Warning: This story contains a graphic image.

The bill for almost $40,000 details the loss of 16 sheep and 145 lambs, as well as the cost of night patrols to protect his flock.

Scott Keller, who farms at Rainbow, on the eastern edge of the Big Desert, says he does not expect the government to pay the invoice, but hopes it will highlight the issue ahead of the November election.

"Something's got to change," he said.

"The invoice has gained a bit of traction and some of the ministers have brought it up in parliament, so it's making a bit of noise."

Scott Keller says wild dog attacks on his livestock have cost him close to $40,000. (Supplied: Scott Keller)

Since March 2024, the lethal control of wild dogs or dingoes in the north-west has been outlawed in order to protect the dingo population.

Mr Keller said predation of his livestock was not a major issue before then because government trappers disposed of problem animals.

"But now [the wild dogs are] getting far more game," he said.

"They're walking probably 8 kilometres from the scrub to find our stock and have a feed on them.

" We've shifted the stock right up to the back of the farmhouse, and they're still getting attacked there. "

Mr Keller said he was concerned about attacks on his working dogs and family pets.

Wild dogs or dingoes have killed hundreds of sheep in north-west Victoria since the government ceased lethal control. (Supplied: Alan Bennett)

Coalition commitment

The state opposition has promised to restore the "unprotection order" that allowed lethal control if it wins government in November.

Shadow Agriculture Minister Emma Kealy said farmers were "at breaking point".

Emma Kealy says the Victorian government has displayed a lack of understanding of the reality for farmers. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

"We had a policy that worked and it didn't make sense at all to remove those protections for stock and farmers," she said.

"Now there are no controls in place and they are running rampant and killing stock in the most cruel way possible.

"It's sheer neglect and lack of understanding of what happens on farms in regional Victoria."

A government spokesperson said compensation was not offered for livestock predation.

"The Victorian Government recognises that Victorian farmers' experience of livestock predation can be distressing and costly, and remains committed to working with farmers, landholders and Traditional Owners to appropriately balance the protection of livestock while maintaining dingo conservation," they said in a statement.

"DEECA, including through Agriculture Victoria and the Vertebrate Species Management Program, is committed to working with farmers impacted by predation in the north west of Victoria."

World.title: Infantino could face UEFA lawsuit as he scrambles for FIFA presidency support
World.content:
European football body UEFA has threatened FIFA with legal action over Gianni Infantino's failed plan to sell a stake in future World Cup profits to private investors, and said any potential evidence should not be destroyed.

Infantino's secretive proposal to raise $US4.2 billion ($6 billion) from investors, including the New York investment firm of Joshua Kushner, was dropped on Saturday, days after media reports revealed it, provoking a global furore.

UEFA led the backlash and its 55 member federations met to agree to boycott all FIFA events and competitions while the proposal was active.

Now UEFA's lawyers have informed FIFA that the European body is "actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints … arising out of and in connection with the FFE (FIFA Forward Enterprise) plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters".

The letter named 18 FIFA executives who it said should retain data, documents and electronic messages as potential evidence. They include Infantino, Zurich-based chief finance officer Thomas Peyer and Arsène Wenger, the coaching great who is FIFA's head of global football development.

Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke Two of football's major bodies launch stinging rebukes of FIFA boss Gianni Infantino after his failed privatisation ploy.

"UEFA puts you on formal notice that any destruction, deletion, alteration, concealment, or loss of relevant materials following receipt of this notice — or following any earlier date on which you were, or reasonably should have been, aware that proceedings were anticipated — may constitute spoliation of evidence," the letter said.

Meanwhile, the Swedish football federation confirmed that UEFA is actively looking "to come up with an alternative candidate" as FIFA president. The next election is scheduled in March.

On Saturday, UEFA signalled it wants to end Infantino's decade-long presidency, saying he had lost the confidence of world football and that "no option should be off the table".

Hours earlier, Infantino had withdrawn the divisive proposal that offered FIFA's 211 member federations one-off payments of $20 million each with a mid-September deadline to accept.

The FFE spin-off valued by FIFA at $20 billion would have taken control of the football body's money-making commercial and tournament operations through at least 2038. It promised to more than double development money over that time for the 211 members who already effectively own the Zurich-based not-for-profit governing body.

It was the project of just one man, FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said in a stinging statement, that said staff felt deceived by their boss Infantino.

FIFA's COO said staff felt "deceived" by Infantino's plan. (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

Legal proceedings are "reasonably anticipated," UEFA's lawyer Andrew J Levander wrote, citing the belief of football stakeholders that the plan was "fundamentally incompatible with the proper governance of football".

UEFA has been outspoken against its former employee Infantino, while the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF also made strong statements opposing Infantino's plan.

Infantino has most support from his traditional base in Africa, while South America's CONMEBOL is relying on him to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams from 48. That would give more hosting games to Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, the home country of CONMEBOL president Alejandro Dominguez.

Gianni Infantino is reportedly seeking support from Donald Trump in his FIFA presidency battle. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Infantino's path to stabilising the presidency he has held for more than 10 years was unclear. A report yesterday claimed he was seeking support from the administration of his close ally US President Donald Trump, possibly in a call with Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"There are no plans for @SecRubio to speak with Infantino and there is no call this morning," Dylan Johnson, assistant secretary of state for global public affairs, posted on social media.

The 56-year-old FIFA leader left New York after the World Cup final two weeks ago seemingly a lock to be re-elected unopposed next March for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

FIFA briefed at the World Cup that Infantino had pledged letters of support from about 200 of the 211 member federations.

Those letters are now likely being withdrawn across Europe, with the Wales federation the first to announce its reversal.

The candidate deadline is November 18 for an election four months later in Morocco.

World.title: Footage emerges of car ploughing through council bus
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity council Footage emerges of car ploughing through council bus Courtney Kruk August 4, 2026 — 8:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Extraordinary footage has emerged of the moment a car became airborne and ploughed through the side of a bus in Brisbane, with the lord mayor praising the quick thinking of the bus’s driver. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner and Public Transport Chair Andrew Wines will inspect the damaged bus on Tuesday at the Sherwood Bus Depot and are expected to speak about the driver’s actions. Loading “The bus driver … he did absolutely the right thing,” Schrinner told ABC Radio. “[He] went straight into action and assisted the driver of the car.



“He’s also a driver that has a really good record with council as well. He’s served for at least seven years and had lots of commendations from the public.” About 6.30pm on Wednesday, a SsangYong being driven by a 66-year-old man attempted to merge from a centre lane and turn off near the intersection of Beaudesert Road and Granard Road in Rocklea. Related Article Public Transport Man fined as police allege cause of car smashing into side of bus A Toyota Yaris being driven by a 45-year-old woman travelling in the outer lane was forced to swerve around the SsangYong, causing the driver to lose control of the vehicle, which became airborne and crashed into the bus. The bus was not in service at the time of the crash.



Its driver, also a 66-year-old man, was not injured, and provided emergency assistance to the trapped driver of the Yaris. “I want to thank the driver for their effort, staying calm and assisting in that situation,” Schrinner said. Police and paramedics arrived at the scene a short time later. The woman was taken to hospital and treated for shock. Following investigations, police issued the SsangYong driver with a traffic infringement notice for driving without due care and attention. It carries a $690 fine and loss of three demerit points. World.title: Qantas mulls offshoring up to 1000 jobs to India: report
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAviation Qantas mulls offshoring up to 1000 jobs to India: report Chris Zappone August 4, 2026 — 7:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Qantas is considering outsourcing up to 1000 roles to India in a major deal with consulting giant Accenture, according to the Australian Financial Review. The airline would consider shifting jobs in marketing, finance, human resources and other back-office positions, the AFR reported, citing people briefed on the matter. Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson has stressed the growing importance of the use of technology at the airline. Bloomberg via Getty Images A final decision on the plan, called Project iQ, is expected this year. A Qantas spokesperson told the AFR the airline was “looking at ways to accelerate the use of technology and AI to help us modernise the way we work and deliver better outcomes for our customers and our people”.

US stocks rallied the edge of their all-time high after easing oil prices helped calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could get even worse. The S&P 500 jumped 1.5 per cent and is just 0.1 per cent below its record set earlier this summer. It’s coming off a wild July, where it swung up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and other worries. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 2.1 per cent. Wall Street has rallied to start the week. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to edge lower, with futures pointing to a loss of 1 point at the open. The ASX jumped 0.5 per cent on Monday after President Donald Trump said over the weekend that he decided to hold off on new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region. US stocks got a lift to kick off their trading week as the price for a barrel of Brent crude sank 5 per cent to $US83.52. Brent’s price careened between $US72 and $US102 last month as worries rose and fell about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude to customers worldwide. United Airlines flew 5.8 per cent higher, while American Airlines climbed 5 per cent. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 6.6 per cent higher. Boeing soared 8 per cent. US regulators certified its new 737 MAX-7 planes, clearing it for commercial service, following years of work to provide pilots with clearer information and warnings, along with other improvements.

World.title: Time travel, punk music and a novel written in one sentence: 13 books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As we head into the final month of winter, you can find stacks of new books popping up in your local bookshop. Here are 13 that might be up your street. Sophie, Standing There

Meg Mason

Fourth Estate, $34.99, out now

Sorrow and Bliss was such a ginormous hit that it really changed the life of New Zealand-born-and-raised author, Meg Mason. It was her second novel, and her third emerged from the considerable success and fame she found with it. Sophie is a sound technician at writers festivals, who in her solitary life becomes obsessed with a particular writer. But this is more than a study of loneliness. As Mason says in the interview that you can read here, she wanted it to be a fast and easy read that name-checks other writers and employs some surprising techniques. Meg Mason’s third novel is more than a study of loneliness. James Brickwood Blackbirding

Ryan Butta

Simon & Schuster, $36.99, out now

The term “blackbirding” refers to the 60,000 Pacific Islanders brought against their will to Australia to work in Queensland’s sugar fields between 1860 and 1906, and the practice is indicative of Australian historical euphemism to “obscure an action that is morally or emotionally or politically problematic”. Ryan Butta tells the stories based on documentation − it is not his right to tell the stories of the enslaved − and the egregious behaviour of the founder of the trade, Robert Towns, and the murderous James Murray is eye-opening and shocking. Time Travel for Beginners

Jaclyn Moriarty

Ultimo, $34.99, out now

Jaclyn Moriarty had the idea for her third novel for adults, and 17th overall, about 20 years ago. At first, it reminded me of the 2019 French film La Belle Epoque. Single mother Anna hates her job at the Nut Bar but, after getting hit by a car, is offered a job as a time travel agent. Clients revisit significant events with the proviso they can’t change anything; meanwhile, other characters converge in Anna’s life. As Moriarty told Lenny Ann Low, “regret is designed to prevent you making mistakes again … the trouble is, it gets jammed in a loop.” Amy Remeikis decries civility politics in her new book. Screw Nice

Amy Remeikis

Hachette, $34.99, out now

Political analyst Amy Remeikis follows her bestselling On Reckoning with a take-down of what she calls “civility politics [that] lets us stand silent while we see someone with less social power than us being bullied in the classroom, society or workplace”. It’s crammed full of examples from Australia and the US of how politicians and commentators have their say, and the way in which they do so makes for a bracing read. Not surprisingly, Remeikis cites Orwell: “If you turn the other cheek, you will get a harder blow on it than you got on the first one.”



Now, Autonomy

Max Easton

Giramondo, $32.95, out now

If you fancy a trip through Sydney subcultures, Max Easton is your guy. In the third of his novels that navigate these worlds, we’re in 2024 and Helen is out of the share-house at the heart of Paradise Estate and in an apartment with Pat, who has secretly unearthed his memoir of life in the early 2000s. Sunny and Sio join them in a year-long lease on a vacant hotel − they call it “The Quarterly” − in which to stage “events” for their tribes and “save Sydney from itself”. But nothing is as simple as it seems, particularly Helen’s relationship with Maria. Nuclear Archipelago

Elizabeth Tynan

NewSouth, $39.99, out now

The third in Elizabeth Tynan’s award-winning trilogy about Britain’s “nuclear colonialism” in Australia details the tests in the Monte Bello Islands in 1952 and 1956 off the Pilbara coast. The latter was by far the “largest bomb ever exploded in Australia”. As Tynan says, “none of the test sites were properly cleaned up … pristine environments such as the Monte Bello Islands were permanently scarred”. The full story remains untold as the British remain “stubbornly secretive”. Tynan reckons “Australians have a right to know exactly what took place on our soil”. Mine

Adam Ouston

Transit Lounge, $$34.99, out now

Don’t be put off by the fact that Adam Ouston’s second novel is written as one sentence. Angel Down, the winner of this year’s Pulitzer for fiction, is also one sentence, but Daniel Kraus breaks it into paragraphs, each of which begins with the word “and”. Readers should trust authors, and Ouston’s digressive prose soon catches you in its rhythms. His narrator is an 80-year-old poet and environmental activist given to procrastination who wants to write a “hauntology” of Tasmania’s West Coast, but has tumbled into a mineshaft, his fall broken by his backpack. He may be trapped, but his mind isn’t and his consciousness roams far and wide. Adam Ouston has written his new novel in one sentence. The Hurt

Catherine de Saint Phalle

Transit Lounge, $32.99, out now

When she was 18 and struggling to survive in a lycee she despised, Catherine de Saint Phalle met Julien who, a few years older than her, “added voice and texture to Paris” with punk music and his black curls. De Saint Phalle previously wrote a memoir about her parents, Poum and Alexandre, and they feature wonderfully here as well. In writing characterised by vivid imagery − “Eighteen wasn’t very old, but I felt my childhood escaping me on roller skates” − de Saint Phalle relates the story of her relationship with Julien, and how writing it led her out of a later “forest of despair”. Realms of Gold

A.J. Mackinnon

Black Inc., $36.99, out August 4

Most people take the car; some travel by trains or boats or planes, and some, such as Patrick Leigh Fermor, like to walk. But if you’re A.J. “Sandy” Mackinnon, you take a small Mirror dinghy and go as far as you can. He recounted his eccentric journey from Shropshire to the Black Sea in the delicious memoir, The Unlikely Voyage of Jack de Crow; 18 years later, he’s back with an account of another intrepid, slightly bonkers, voyage in a similar dinghy, this time from the port in Romania where the first vessel ended up to Venice. Eye of the Needle

Christopher Raja

Text, $34.99, out August 4

The end of innocence was a key theme of Christopher Raja’s first novel, The Burning Elephant. You could say Eye of the Needle has a similar focus, as one of his two narrators, Kris, a would-be writer in 1990s Melbourne, turns his back on family and slips into the dismal world of heroin addiction, while the other, Kadir, an Afghan cameleer on a scientific expedition venturing into the desert from Beltana in 1882, has his eyes opened about colonialism and its brutal consequences for the Indigenous population. But who is telling Kadir’s story?

Extraordinary footage has emerged of the moment a car became airborne and ploughed through the side of a bus in Brisbane, with the lord mayor praising the quick thinking of the bus’s driver. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner and Public Transport Chair Andrew Wines will inspect the damaged bus on Tuesday at the Sherwood Bus Depot and are expected to speak about the driver’s actions. Loading “The bus driver … he did absolutely the right thing,” Schrinner told ABC Radio. “[He] went straight into action and assisted the driver of the car.



“He’s also a driver that has a really good record with council as well. He’s served for at least seven years and had lots of commendations from the public.” About 6.30pm on Wednesday, a SsangYong being driven by a 66-year-old man attempted to merge from a centre lane and turn off near the intersection of Beaudesert Road and Granard Road in Rocklea. Related Article Public Transport Man fined as police allege cause of car smashing into side of bus A Toyota Yaris being driven by a 45-year-old woman travelling in the outer lane was forced to swerve around the SsangYong, causing the driver to lose control of the vehicle, which became airborne and crashed into the bus. The bus was not in service at the time of the crash.



Its driver, also a 66-year-old man, was not injured, and provided emergency assistance to the trapped driver of the Yaris. “I want to thank the driver for their effort, staying calm and assisting in that situation,” Schrinner said. Police and paramedics arrived at the scene a short time later. The woman was taken to hospital and treated for shock. Following investigations, police issued the SsangYong driver with a traffic infringement notice for driving without due care and attention. It carries a $690 fine and loss of three demerit points. World.title: Time travel, punk music and a novel written in one sentence: 13 books to read this month
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

As we head into the final month of winter, you can find stacks of new books popping up in your local bookshop. Here are 13 that might be up your street. Sophie, Standing There

Meg Mason

Fourth Estate, $34.99, out now

Sorrow and Bliss was such a ginormous hit that it really changed the life of New Zealand-born-and-raised author, Meg Mason. It was her second novel, and her third emerged from the considerable success and fame she found with it. Sophie is a sound technician at writers festivals, who in her solitary life becomes obsessed with a particular writer. But this is more than a study of loneliness. As Mason says in the interview that you can read here, she wanted it to be a fast and easy read that name-checks other writers and employs some surprising techniques. Meg Mason’s third novel is more than a study of loneliness. James Brickwood Blackbirding

Ryan Butta

Simon & Schuster, $36.99, out now

The term “blackbirding” refers to the 60,000 Pacific Islanders brought against their will to Australia to work in Queensland’s sugar fields between 1860 and 1906, and the practice is indicative of Australian historical euphemism to “obscure an action that is morally or emotionally or politically problematic”. Ryan Butta tells the stories based on documentation − it is not his right to tell the stories of the enslaved − and the egregious behaviour of the founder of the trade, Robert Towns, and the murderous James Murray is eye-opening and shocking. Time Travel for Beginners

Jaclyn Moriarty

Ultimo, $34.99, out now

Jaclyn Moriarty had the idea for her third novel for adults, and 17th overall, about 20 years ago. At first, it reminded me of the 2019 French film La Belle Epoque. Single mother Anna hates her job at the Nut Bar but, after getting hit by a car, is offered a job as a time travel agent. Clients revisit significant events with the proviso they can’t change anything; meanwhile, other characters converge in Anna’s life. As Moriarty told Lenny Ann Low, “regret is designed to prevent you making mistakes again … the trouble is, it gets jammed in a loop.” Amy Remeikis decries civility politics in her new book. Screw Nice

Amy Remeikis

Hachette, $34.99, out now

Political analyst Amy Remeikis follows her bestselling On Reckoning with a take-down of what she calls “civility politics [that] lets us stand silent while we see someone with less social power than us being bullied in the classroom, society or workplace”. It’s crammed full of examples from Australia and the US of how politicians and commentators have their say, and the way in which they do so makes for a bracing read. Not surprisingly, Remeikis cites Orwell: “If you turn the other cheek, you will get a harder blow on it than you got on the first one.”



Now, Autonomy

Max Easton

Giramondo, $32.95, out now

If you fancy a trip through Sydney subcultures, Max Easton is your guy. In the third of his novels that navigate these worlds, we’re in 2024 and Helen is out of the share-house at the heart of Paradise Estate and in an apartment with Pat, who has secretly unearthed his memoir of life in the early 2000s. Sunny and Sio join them in a year-long lease on a vacant hotel − they call it “The Quarterly” − in which to stage “events” for their tribes and “save Sydney from itself”. But nothing is as simple as it seems, particularly Helen’s relationship with Maria. Nuclear Archipelago

Elizabeth Tynan

NewSouth, $39.99, out now

The third in Elizabeth Tynan’s award-winning trilogy about Britain’s “nuclear colonialism” in Australia details the tests in the Monte Bello Islands in 1952 and 1956 off the Pilbara coast. The latter was by far the “largest bomb ever exploded in Australia”. As Tynan says, “none of the test sites were properly cleaned up … pristine environments such as the Monte Bello Islands were permanently scarred”. The full story remains untold as the British remain “stubbornly secretive”. Tynan reckons “Australians have a right to know exactly what took place on our soil”. Mine

Adam Ouston

Transit Lounge, $$34.99, out now

Don’t be put off by the fact that Adam Ouston’s second novel is written as one sentence. Angel Down, the winner of this year’s Pulitzer for fiction, is also one sentence, but Daniel Kraus breaks it into paragraphs, each of which begins with the word “and”. Readers should trust authors, and Ouston’s digressive prose soon catches you in its rhythms. His narrator is an 80-year-old poet and environmental activist given to procrastination who wants to write a “hauntology” of Tasmania’s West Coast, but has tumbled into a mineshaft, his fall broken by his backpack. He may be trapped, but his mind isn’t and his consciousness roams far and wide. Adam Ouston has written his new novel in one sentence. The Hurt

Catherine de Saint Phalle

Transit Lounge, $32.99, out now

When she was 18 and struggling to survive in a lycee she despised, Catherine de Saint Phalle met Julien who, a few years older than her, “added voice and texture to Paris” with punk music and his black curls. De Saint Phalle previously wrote a memoir about her parents, Poum and Alexandre, and they feature wonderfully here as well. In writing characterised by vivid imagery − “Eighteen wasn’t very old, but I felt my childhood escaping me on roller skates” − de Saint Phalle relates the story of her relationship with Julien, and how writing it led her out of a later “forest of despair”. Realms of Gold

A.J. Mackinnon

Black Inc., $36.99, out August 4

Most people take the car; some travel by trains or boats or planes, and some, such as Patrick Leigh Fermor, like to walk. But if you’re A.J. “Sandy” Mackinnon, you take a small Mirror dinghy and go as far as you can. He recounted his eccentric journey from Shropshire to the Black Sea in the delicious memoir, The Unlikely Voyage of Jack de Crow; 18 years later, he’s back with an account of another intrepid, slightly bonkers, voyage in a similar dinghy, this time from the port in Romania where the first vessel ended up to Venice. Eye of the Needle

Christopher Raja

Text, $34.99, out August 4

The end of innocence was a key theme of Christopher Raja’s first novel, The Burning Elephant. You could say Eye of the Needle has a similar focus, as one of his two narrators, Kris, a would-be writer in 1990s Melbourne, turns his back on family and slips into the dismal world of heroin addiction, while the other, Kadir, an Afghan cameleer on a scientific expedition venturing into the desert from Beltana in 1882, has his eyes opened about colonialism and its brutal consequences for the Indigenous population. But who is telling Kadir’s story?

World.title: Wild deer costing Hawke's Bay farmers tens of thousands of dollars - study
World.content:
Study reveals cost of wild deer damage Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A new study of wild deer populations in Hawke's Bay has found the problem is costing farmers tens of thousands of dollars.

The research, by primary sector economist Peter MacIntyre, reveals extensive pasture and crop losses from deer, as well as damage to native plantings and bush.

He said wild deer may be causing far greater economic damage to farms than many landowners realise.

"There is good evidence from drone and helicopter thermal imaging that many landowners could have five to six times more deer than they think.

"Once deer numbers grow from 50 to 100 and more, the economic damage gets significant, more so if they are getting 100 percent of their feed from your property," said MacIntyre.

Porangahau farmer Sam Stoddart is all too familiar with the problem, with 8000 hectares of bush on his farm boundary.

"There'd be at an estimate... 800 plus deer right on our boundary, so a young kale crop will get pulled.. plucked out before it's had time to establish," said Stoddart.

He said if those 800 deer grazed on his land they'd eat about the same amount as 1200 sheep, which could be making him $145,000 a year.

Instead, with hundreds of wild deer creeping onto his land, the farmer has paddocks he can't put into higher value crops, winter grass that's being chewed up and native plants that are disappearing.

He said wild deer populations have ballooned over the past 10 years or so.

"The numbers have just exploded. They were released as a bit of game for hunters but were never really controlled I don't think by DOC [Department of Conservation] or anything... now it's got to stage where we need some sort of government intervention," said Stoddart.

Wild deer in the Central Hawke's Bay village of Pōrangahau. Supplied

He's one of 14 landowners that rural economist Peter MacIntyre talked to for his research into the wild deer problem in Hawke's Bay.

"It was a rather depressing story. People had lost a lot of natives, people were losing forage crops," said MacIntyre.

"It was a pretty sobering story from everybody."

The research was organised by Marie Taylor from Plant Hawke's Bay and funded by the Hawke's Bay Regional Council, the Joan Fernie Charitable Trust and the Pan Pac Environmental Trust.

During the study, one landowner who thought he had 50 deer on his property found nearly 300 with thermal imaging - and Taylor said this highlighted how huge the wild deer problem had become.

"Numbers have increased really exponentially. They are a real limiting factor for all things on farm including plantings, they're also really totalling our biodversity because they graze species by species, they take most palatable things out of the landscape first.

"Even though the canopy of the forest looks great, we are losing everything underneath," she said.

The study showed when 100 deer got half of their annual feed requirements from productive pasture, farmers lost more than $10,000 per year.

MacIntyre said over 10 years, using an 8.4 percent discount rate, that was more than $100,000 in lost value.

"If farmers are losing forage or won't plant forage because of the likely damage, you can more than double the losses above."

Wild deer on the run in New Zealand Department of Conservation

'I want to see people working together'

MacIntyre said new deer fences cost in the vicinity of $40,000 per kilometre and sustained shooting programmes were costly and required ongoing effort. He calculated that electric fencing added to existing fences, would be less, at around $8000 per kilometre.

However, he said when you took into account the losses from deer grazing, it becomes more economically viable to fence.

"If you try to ringfence your farm it's going to cost you quite a lot... If you gang up with your neighbours and ringfence off the problem area then it's going to be a lot more cost effective for each farmer," he said.

Taylor agreed.

"We need to work as catchment goups and put up deer fencing where we can defend the fence. I want to see people working together like they did with possum control areas - that was hugely successful in Hawke's Bay," said Taylor.

But she said to achieve that, what is really needed is more funding for conservation and pest control.

"There has been an uncontrolled invasion of feral deer into farmed land from the ranges in Hawke's Bay with no coordinated control programmes and a consequent destruction of years of careful biodiversity planning, planting and management as well as economic loss to farmers.

"Unless DOC does its job properly this situation will only get worse with deer numbers increasing and environmental damage becoming even more significant and economic costs to farmers becoming unsustainable," she said.

Wild deer can be found in both the North and South Islands of New Zealand on public conservation land and private property. Supplied

The Department of Convservation's wild animals manager, Mike Perry, told RNZ that DOC actively managed deer in areas where they had the greatest impact on biodiversity, with around 200,000 hectares of deer management undertaken nationwide.

"We acknowledge that wild animal numbers are increasing. National monitoring shows ungulates (wild deer, goats, pigs, chamois and tahr) are present at approximately 83 percent of monitored sites on public conservation land, up from 63 percent in 2013.

"In response, DOC has significantly increased control efforts across the country in recent years through additional funding provided in Budget 2022, alongside more than $10 million received through the International Visitor Levy," said Perry.

DOC said deer management is carried out at several sites across Hawke's Bay and surrounding areas, such as in the Ruahine Forest Part.

However, Perry said in Hawke's Bay wild goats posed a greater ecological threat than deer in many conservation areas.

"DOC undertakes goat control across a range of sites in the region and is carrying out extensive work in the northeastern Ruahine Range with the goal of making that part of the park wild goat free."

He said managing wild animals is a shared responsibility that extended beyond public conservation land.

World.title: In-school teacher training programmes are a ' system disruptor' - Stanford
World.content:
In-school teacher training programmes are a "disruptor" that will help improve initial teacher education, says the education minister.

The government has announced it will increase the number of funded places from 528 this year to 660 next year and 704 every year from 2028.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the increase would cost $21.7m over five years and the funding was redirected from a relocation grant for foreign early childhood teachers.

Students on the School Onsite Training Programme are placed three days a week in a host school and are paid a $20,660 bursary while they complete a one-year teaching qualification.

Stanford said it was a good option for students straight out of university and for career-changers.

Asked if the government wanted the model to become the dominant or preferred form of teacher education, Stanford said it would depend on the programme's success.

"We do need to do an evaluation at a later date, once we've had a few years under our belt. But it is certainly proving to be very successful," she said.

"All of the schools I talk to absolutely love it. They love the teachers who come out the other end because they're so much more prepared to teach in the classroom.

"So it is something I would like to keep investing in if the statistics show that it is working."

Universities recently told RNZ they felt out of favour because non-universities were allocated significant increases in funded places under the scheme, but they were not.

"They are not out of favour," Stanford said.

"There's a criteria. Meet the criteria and you'll get places. It's as simple as that."

But Stanford said initial teacher education needed a shake-up, citing a 2024 Education Review Office report that said many new teachers were not well-prepared for their job.

Universities have [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/education/516698/universities-reject-ero-criticism-of-teacher-training-courses

criticised the report], saying it was completed after Covid lock-downs disrupted many students' classroom placements and the principals unhappy with the quality of graduates were not a representative sample.

"You will have seen ERO's report into the ability of teachers to manage classroom behaviour and be ready to teach, and they have made many comments about the state of initial teacher education," she said.

"There isn't a day of the week that I don't go into a school and have a principal say to me that they lament the state of initial teacher education in this country. I make no apologies that this is a system disruptor.

"It's part of the reason I'm taking the initial teacher education standard setting function off the teaching council, putting it with the Ministry of Education because we want to up the standards to make sure that the graduates are coming out and it's to be fair to them as well.

World.title: National MPs back Luxon over his apology to businesses
World.content:
Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 6m

National Party MPs are backing their leader over his apology to businesses, but won't say whether Winston Peters should be sacked for comments aimed at a Chinese-born MP.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has apologised on Monday for comments deemed "out of touch" by some, after he told an audience at a Rotorua Business Chamber event last week that some businesses had a "parent-child mentality" and too often looked to the government for help.

He also said he had [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/875148/luxon-speaks-to-peters-about-comments-that-s-a-conversation-between-us

spoken with Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters] about telling the Greens' Lawrence Xu-nan to go back to his own country - comments Luxon called "racist" - but refused to outline what exactly was discussed.

Answering questions outside of Parliament on Tuesday morning, Rangitīkei MP Suze Redmayne said the Christopher Luxon was out with business owners most weeks.

"Just by his actions, he supports small businesses 100 percent."

"He's out and about visiting businesses every week, including a couple of weeks ago [when] I took them to Mitchpine in Levin, where they were effusive in their praise." she said.

Asked whether she was comfortable with Peters serving in a Cabinet propped up by her party's votes, Redmayne said "it's not my Cabinet".

Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Banks Peninsula MP Vanessa Weenink said Peter's comments were racist and some of her constituents were "upset" by them but would not say whether he should lose his position.

"That's something that the prime minister should answer to and has discussed - it's not up to me," she said.

West Coast-Tasman MP Maureen Pugh admitted she had not seen Luxon's apology because she left her phone in Wellington over the weekend.

Pugh said Peters' comments were "ill-conceived" but when asked if she was surprised the that prime minister still supported Peters' to be foreign minister, she did not answer directly.

"We're in the downhill slope now of a three-year term. Let's just see out the last six weeks," she said.

Similarly, List MP Nancy Lu said she thought the comments were racist, but avoided questions on Peters.

Deputy PM Seymour on Luxon apology, infrastructure spending First Up Download MP3 5m

It was the same from Upper Harbour MP Cameron Brewer, who said he was focused on other things.

"We are focused in these last few weeks on passing some key legislation, mainly around the Resource Management Act.

"It's been made clear that the prime minister has said that yes, those comments were racist, and we wish to move on."

Southland MP Joseph Mooney said everyone was responsible for their own words.

"The prime minister has made his his own views on those comments very clear... there's not much more to say really than that," he said.

Luxon misread the room - Labour leader

Labour leader Chris Hipkins told Morning Report the Prime Minister had misread the room when he told Rotorua small business owners that they had a "parent-child mentality".

Hipkins said small businesses were important to the New Zealand economy, and he understood the personal contribution and sacrifice they made.

"When they raise legitimate concerns with the prime minister, as they did last week, they deserve to be respected and treated seriously, not spoken to as if they're children and I think the prime minister has totally misread the room there."

Asked if he thought Labour could win the votes of small businesses, Hipkins said his party was going all out to win those votes.

ACT leader David Seymour told First Up it was up to the prime minister as to whether or not he decided to apologise.

"He obviously felt he had been misunderstood or perhaps misspoken what he was trying to get across and he'd caused some offence to some people, so he apologised and good on him."

World.title: All Blacks hooker George Bell ruled out of South Africa tour
World.content:
Hooker George Bell has been ruled out of the All Blacks tour of South Africa and has been replaced by Bradley Slater.

Bell was the fourth hooker named in the squad of 44 late last month.

The 24-year-old suffered a calf strain during training in Cape Town this week and will return home.

He's expected to be out of action for four to six weeks.

Taranaki and Blues hooker Bradley Slater is due to arrive in South Africa in the next 24 hours.

"We are all gutted for George, to be ruled out of the tour so early," All Blacks Head Coach Dave Rennie said.

"He's had a frustrating past few months with injury so it's a real blow for him to have injured his calf again. We look forward to seeing him return via the NPC and put himself in a position to push for All Blacks selection later in the year."

Bell played four tests for New Zealand in 2024 and 2025.

Bradley Slater playing for the Blues Clay Cross / PHOTOSPORT

Bradley Slater is the son of Taranaki rugby legend Andy Slater while three cap All Black Gordon Slater is his uncle.

The 27-year-old played for the Chiefs between 2019 and 2025 and moved to the Blues this year.

The played fo the All Blacks XV in 2024 and 2025.

World.title: No need for Luxon to apologise over Rotorua business meeting comments, mayor says
World.content:
Rotorua Business Chamber responds to PM’s apology Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The Rotorua mayor says the prime minister's comments to a business audience last week were him being honest, and she doesn't think he needed to apologise.

"I don't think it's a time for our leaders in New Zealand to be soft. We need to know the truth. We need to be honest, and we need to set a pathway forward," National party-aligned Tania Tapsell said.

Meanwhile, the Rotorua Business Chamber is welcoming the apology from Christopher Luxon, but hoped there's "genuine reflection behind it".

Luxon had told the audience at a Rotorua Business Chamber event on Friday that some businesses had a "parent-child mentality" and too often looked to the government for help.

His office later released a transcript.

Craig McCulloch on PM’s apology to business owners Morning Report Download MP3 5m

On Monday, he apologised, saying he was sorry his comments "did not properly acknowledge the challenges that many small business owners are facing".

"I didn't want to cause any offence. That's not what I intended to do."

President of the Rotorua Business Chamber Paul Ingram welcomed the apology, but hoped there was "genuine reflection behind it".

Ingram told RNZ small and medium businesses were the backbone of the New Zealand economy, and it was important that the sector was taken seriously by "every government".

Rotorua Business Chamber president Paul Ingram. Supplied / Rotorua Business Chamber

"Because collectively we have the ability to enable the growth and success that we're collectively looking for.

"I don't think we're looking for a handout. We're looking for understanding," Ingram added.

The reflection he wanted Luxon to consider was that there was an understanding of what these business owners were going through.

He acknowledged some of the comments last week may have been "unintended", or as "sharp and as pointed as they were", and he understood the prime minister came from a business background.

But he hoped there'd be a consideration that whatever was going on in the economy translated into what was real for New Zealand businesses.

"For mum and dad businesses that have got a mortgage, the house is on the line."

In welcoming the apology, Ingram said he would look forward to seeing what actions the government would take now to support small businesses going forward.

Overall Ingram said other parts of the discussion he "totally" agreed with, it was just the "whole parent-child narrative that came out that didn't really land very well".

The Rotorua mayor told RNZ the business community really appreciated having the prime minister in town.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tapsell was the National Party candidate for the East Coast electorate in 2020.

She acknowledged it was "tough times, and that was the context in which the question was answered".

She said Luxon didn't need to apologise because "he had a room full of people that was taking on his advice".

Tapsell, who wasn't at the event herself, was told that the feeling in the room afterwards was "definitely that they appreciated his thoughts on it".

"We need to get real in New Zealand," Tapsell said. "Sometimes it is us that actually needs to solve our own problems, and I feel like that's what he's doing not only in those comments but also actually in Parliament.

"So good on him."

Tapsell said Luxon was being honest, and that was "the best thing we can ask from people".

"At least he's not running us around in a circle, not answering the question, and honestly, that was appreciated and valued on the day in the room."

She said it was "very lovely" that he did apologise, and reflected Luxon's honesty and integrity, "he's being honest as he was in the room".

"It's a pretty big thing for a politician to apologise. This doesn't happen very often."

Tapsell said from the business perspective, he was answering a question in the context of difficult times.

"Yes, things are bad, but don't rely on government handouts - I can understand that as a mayor from a council as well.

World.title: Labour leader Chris Hipkins rules out working with Winston Peters as foreign affairs minister
World.content:
Weekly interview with opposition leader, Chris Hipkins Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has ruled out working with New Zealand First's Winston Peters at the next election.

New Zealand First's leader responded to heckling in the House on Wednesday last week by attacking the Greens' Lawrence Xu-nan, telling him to go back to his "own country".

Hipkins said Winston Peters' position as foreign affairs minister was completely untenable.

"He's making international headlines for all the wrong reasons. He can't continue in that job, he can't credibly represent New Zealand on the world stage."

Hipkins said he ruled out working with Winston Peters and New Zealand First before the last election and he had not regretted it.

"Behaviour like we've seen with Winston Peters and Shane Jones as well with his racist comments towards Indians in recent months is not compatible with the sort of government I want to lead."

Quilae Wong rules out working with Peters as Foreign Minister Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Asked if he would rule out having Winston Peters as a foreign affairs minister if he led the next government, Hipkins said he could not be foreign affairs minister in any government.

"He cannot represent New Zealand credibly on the world stage when he's making outwardly racist comments."

Asked whether he could work with New Zealand First, Hipkins said "we couldn't work with them at the last election, nothing really has changed that makes this more likely at the coming election."

Peters has already ruled out forming a government with Labour at the next election.

Speaking at a post-Cabinet media conference on Monday afternoon, Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said he had spoken to Peters about the comments, but refused to outline what exactly was discussed, nor would he say whether he expressed disappointment in his foreign minister.

Earlier on Monday, Luxon told Morning Report that Peters' comments were racist but that he had not yet spoken to Peters directly.

At the media conference Luxon would not say if he would have Peters as foreign minister again if he won the election, saying that was all "hypothetical", nor would he be drawn on questions about the risk to coalition stability if Luxon were to discipline or try fire Peters.

Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong has also said her party would not support a government that had Peters as foreign minister.

"As we've always said, we will sit down and try to find common ground, and that remains the case with New Zealand First," she said.

World.title: Who's feeling job market recovery? And where has downturn hit hardest?
World.content:
What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

It has been a tough few years to be a jobseeker. Data this week is expected to show the unemployment rate still hovering around the highest level it's been in a decade.

But fortunes have varied depending on where you are in the country, and the type of work you do.

The job market peak was reached in October 2023, when there were 2.395 million filled jobs nationwide. The trough was in October last year, when that had dropped to 2.337m.

Provisional estimates are that the number is now about 2.35m filled jobs.

Westpac chief economist on fuel prices and unemployment Morning Report Download MP3 6m

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said from the peak of the market to the bottom, there were just under 60,000 jobs lost but since then, 17,575 have been recovered, leaving the country still 40,924 jobs short compared to the busiest time in the labour market.

Here are some of the winners and losers of the labour market both since the peak, and over the past five years.

Sectors

Since the job market peaked in October 2023, the biggest drop in jobs in percentage terms has been felt in the information media and telecommunications sector, down 11.2 percent or 3761 jobs.

Over five years, smoothing out the post-Covid high, job numbers in that sector are still down 5.6 percent.

Construction has also had a sharp fall from the peak, having lost 8.4 percent of its jobs, or 17,249, but the number is flat compared to 2021.

Some sectors have continued to grow since the peak, such as arts and recreation services, which is up 6.1 percent from 2023 and 16.2 percent over five years. Of this sector, the largest proportion of jobs is in sports and physical recreation, such as people working in gyms. Their numbers have lifted from 22,700 in 2023 to 24,400 last year. There has also been significant growth in businesses. Personal health and fitness training business numbers increased 112.5 percent between 2019 and 2025.

Who's feeling job market recovery? Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Healthcare and social assistance jobs have also increased since the job market peak, up 5.4 percent since 2023 and 12.7 percent from five years ago.

Education and training is up 4.4 percent from the peak and 6.6 percent over five years.

Eaqub said, on a per population basis, there had not yet been any real recovery. Data would show there were more hours being worked, he said, but the recovery in jobs so far had only kept pace with population growth. "It's not a high-quality recovery yet."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. RNZ

Construction's increase was the largest in number terms, followed by manufacturing down 11,822.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the strongest parts of the labour market were those that were tied to underlying population growth.

"It's the expansion of certain elements of public service-related industries as well, particularly in health, education… those sectors have grown a lot because the population has grown in the last five years. They've continued to grow, albeit at a slower rate since 2023, because that was when the population growth peaked… there's quite a few industries that are a lot more government or public sector dominated, and they just tend to not be really influenced by the cycle so much."

In contrast, sectors such as construction were much more closely tied to the fortunes of the wider economy.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said the October 2023 peak was exaggerated by the election, with a burst of short-term filled jobs in public administration. "Excluding that boost, jobs activity likely peaked around March 2024."

"The large increases in healthcare, public administration, and education and training reflect a growing population and of course one of the largest health-related events in memory.

"Further hiring in education is also likely due to retraining of people throughout the pandemic, and then as the unemployment rate increased, with more people looking at training options to re- or up-skill."

He said construction had gone through a significant period of change.

"At one point, residential construction intentions were the highest in half a century, fuelled by rocketing house prices and low interest rates, and the sector scaled up to meet that high demand. But when interest rates rose and house prices and activity dropped, construction activity pulled back too, having upped capacity to meet peak needs that just didn't, and were never going to, persist."

He said both admin and information media and telecoms jobs had been holding up for a while until the downturn became more pronounced.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

By age

Young people have experienced the biggest impact of the downturn.

There are now 61,009 fewer jobs held by people aged under 30 than there were at the peak, and 43,726 fewer than five years ago.

The number of people over 55 working has increased 9.7 percent over five years and the number aged 30 to 54 has increased 9.1 percent.

"It's definitely the younger people who had quite a big increase, particularly the 15 to 19-year-olds had a big increase in jobs or employment during that really tight labour market period, when there was a hiring frenzy during the Covid years, those numbers were unusually high.

"The cost of living particularly for necessities skyrocketed so a lot of young people, kids at school, started to work and that's kind of fallen off and hasn't really recovered."

Ministry of Social Development data shows the biggest increase in main benefit recipient numbers has been in the 25 to 39 age group where there are now 20 percent more people receiving a benefit than there were in June 2021.

Eckhold said it was a "no hire, no fire" market.

"We haven't necessarily seen enormous amounts of layoffs in aggregate across the economy, but it has become quite hard to find a job. And that's particularly impacted the younger age group, because they've got less skills and experience, so it's always just a bit harder."

Region

Canterbury has had some of the strongest job growth. Its job numbers are up 1.4 percent compared to the peak and 8.9 percent over five years.

Auckland is down 2.7 percent form the peak and 5.1 percent up over five years.

Wellington is down 3.8 percent from the peak and 0.3 percent up over five years.

Gisborne has been hard hit, down 4.2 percent from the peak and 1.5 percent over five years.

Wellington and Auckland have had the largest percentage increase in benefit recipients between June 2021 and June 2026, in percentage terms.

Eckhold said he expected to see a small increase in the unemployment rate this week and his current forecast was for that to be the peak.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"I will say though, we'll be doing a whole new set of forecasts this month. When we put in place our previous forecasts, it was in the context of a better outlook, because it looked like energy prices were quite a lot lower. It looked like we're going to have a period of more stability, and that seems to have tended not to be the case now that we've got a little bit further on. So, it may be optimistic to expect that the unemployment rate will be peaking now. Perhaps we might have to wait a bit longer for that."

He said the job market would be the last thing to pick up.

"GDP has actually been picking up now for three or four quarters or so. It looks like we had an interruption to growth in Q2, but three quarters before that we'd had some decent growth. But there's always a lag between when you actually see growth occur and then when hiring really picks up.

"Probably at the start of the year, we would have expected that hiring growth to really be starting to hit its straps now, in the second half of the year. But I think the Iran war has really just pushed that back."

World.title: 'Lot of nonsense': Dearden clears air on Cowboys future
World.content:
North Queensland co-captain Tom Dearden has cleared the air about his future and given the club a boost as he targets returning from injury to inspire a finals run.

At the end of the 2023 season Dearden, 26, signed a five-year contract extension through to the end of 2029.

But multiple reports in recent weeks linked him to an early exit for personal reasons due to his pregnant partner, Millie Over, living in Sydney.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Dearden fronted the media to refute the reports due to the impact they were having on his personal life.

"There's been a fair bit of speculation getting around at the moment. There's been a lot of suggestions that I wanted to move or leave the club," Dearden said.
